_about: Worked practice problems for CMPSCI 311 (Kleinberg & Tardos), written to match the course sections. A question is problems[i] (warm-up, a picture-by-picture walk, why it works) plus practice[i] (on your own: picture, hint, answer). Add new ones to both lists at the same position; run test_cs311_bank.py to check them.

intro.big_idea: Pair n colleges with n students so that no college and student would both rather ditch their partners for each other. A pairing with no such 'unstable pair' is called stable, and Gale-Shapley always finds one in O(n^2) time.
intro.picture_this: Admissions day: the matching is stable if no college and student would both rather be with each other than with the partners they ended up with.
you_know_it_when: Two groups, and everyone ranks the people in the other group
You want pairs where nobody has a reason to break away
Words like 'stable', 'preferences', 'offers', 'rejects', 'trades up'

panels.caption: Unstable: a and 2 like each other more than their partners, so they'd break away together.
Stable: no pair would both rather switch. Everyone stays put.

problems.title: Run Gale-Shapley by hand
problems.problem: Colleges a: 1 > 2 > 3, b: 1 > 3 > 2, c: 2 > 1 > 3. Students 1: b > a > c, 2: a > c > b, 3: c > a > b (best first). Run college-proposing Gale-Shapley, always letting the alphabetically first free college make the next offer. List every offer and give the final matching.

visual.caption: Each list is best first. Nobody is matched yet.

warmup.question: Student 1's list is b > a > c, and she currently holds a. College b makes her an offer. Does she accept? What if c makes her an offer instead?
warmup.answer: She accepts b: b is to the left of a, so she trades up and a becomes free. She rejects c: c is to the right of a.

walk.say: Offer 1. a is the first free college, so it offers to its top choice, student 1. She is free, and a free student accepts any offer. Match (a, 1).

visual.caption: offer 1: a -> 1, accepted

walk.look: Notice: brackets mark each person's current partner on their list.

walk.say: Offer 2. b is now the first free college. It also offers to student 1. Her list is b > [a] > c, so b beats a. She trades up to b, and a is free again.

visual.caption: offer 2: b -> 1, she trades up; a is free

walk.look: Notice: a turns coral. It lost its partner and goes back to making offers.

walk.say: Offer 3. a is the first free college. Student 1 is used up, so a moves one step down its list to student 2. She is free: match (a, 2).

visual.caption: offer 3: a -> 2, accepted

walk.look: Notice: a never goes back to student 1. Colleges only move down their lists (F2).

walk.say: Offer 4. c, the only free college, offers to its top choice, student 2. Her list is [a] > c > b, so she keeps a and rejects c.

visual.caption: offer 4: c -> 2, rejected

walk.look: Notice: c is to the right of her bracket, so she says no.

walk.say: Offer 5. c tries its second choice, student 1. Her list is [b] > a > c. She holds her first choice, so she rejects c too.

visual.caption: offer 5: c -> 1, rejected

walk.say: Offer 6. c tries its last choice, student 3. She is free, so she accepts: (c, 3). Every college is matched, so the algorithm stops.

visual.caption: offer 6: c -> 3, accepted; everyone matched

walk.say: Result after 6 offers: {(a, 2), (b, 1), (c, 3)}. Student 1 traded up from a to b. College a slid from its first choice to its second, and c ended on its last.

visual.caption: Final matching: (a, 2), (b, 1), (c, 3).

walk.look: Notice: the faded lines are gone. Only the matches still standing count.

problems.why: Gale-Shapley ends when every college is matched, and the matching it ends with is always stable. Quick check: b holds its first choice; a wants 1, but 1 holds her favorite b; c wants 2 or 1, but 2 prefers her a and 1 prefers her b. No pair wants to switch.
problems.tip: Write each partner in brackets on the lists as you go. A new offer wins only if it is to the LEFT of her bracket.

problems.title: Check a matching for unstable pairs
problems.problem: Colleges a: 2 > 1 > 3, b: 2 > 3 > 1, c: 2 > 1 > 3. Students 1: b > c > a, 2: c > a > b, 3: c > a > b (best first). Someone hands you M = {(a, 2), (b, 1), (c, 3)}. Find every unstable pair. Is M stable?

visual.caption: M = {(a, 2), (b, 1), (c, 3)}, with each partner in brackets.

warmup.question: College c prefers student s to its partner. But s prefers her own partner to c. Is (c, s) an unstable pair?
warmup.answer: No. An unstable pair needs BOTH sides to prefer each other to their partners. One-sided wanting is not enough.

walk.say: Circle every partner first: the brackets on the lists. Anyone to the LEFT of someone's bracket is a person they would rather have. Only those pairs can be unstable.

visual.caption: Partners in brackets.

walk.look: Notice: a's bracket is at the far left. a wants nobody else.

walk.say: Go college by college. a holds 2, its first choice, so a would never switch. No pair with a can be unstable. Skip a.

visual.caption: a is happy: skip it.

walk.say: b holds 1, the last on its list 2 > 3 > [1], so b would like 2 or 3. Test (b, 2): student 2's list is c > [a] > b. She prefers her a. Not unstable.

visual.caption: (b, 2): only b wants it.

walk.look: Notice: b sits to the right of 2's bracket, so she says no.

walk.say: Test (b, 3): student 3's list is [c] > a > b. She holds her first choice, so she would never switch. Not unstable.

visual.caption: (b, 3): 3 is happy.

walk.say: c holds 3, last on its list 2 > 1 > [3], so c would like 2 or 1. Test (c, 2): student 2's list is c > [a] > b. She ranks c above a. Both want it: UNSTABLE.

visual.caption: (c, 2): both sides want the switch.

walk.look: Notice: c is left of 2's bracket AND 2 is left of c's bracket.

walk.say: Finish the list, since the question asks for every pair. Test (c, 1): student 1's list is [b] > c > a. She holds her first choice. Not unstable.

visual.caption: (c, 1): 1 is happy.

walk.say: Result: exactly one unstable pair, (c, 2). So M is not stable: c and student 2 would both break their deals to be together.

visual.caption: One unstable pair, (c, 2). M is not stable.

problems.why: An unstable pair needs both people to prefer each other, so you only test the people each college likes MORE than its partner, then ask whether she likes that college more than hers. Anyone holding a first choice can never be part of an unstable pair, so skip them right away.
problems.tip: Bracket each partner, then test only names to the left of a college's bracket. A pair is unstable only if each is left of the other's bracket.

problems.title: Why Gale-Shapley stops, and why it is O(n^2)
problems.problem: Show that Gale-Shapley makes at most n^2 offers when there are n colleges and n students, and explain how to run it in O(n^2) total time. Use the run from the first worked example (6 offers) as your picture.

visual.caption: One box per possible offer (college, student): n x n = 9 boxes.

warmup.question: A college offers down its list and never offers to the same student twice. With 4 colleges and 4 students, how many different (college, student) offers are even possible?
warmup.answer: 4 x 4 = 16. So no run with n = 4 can ever make more than 16 offers.

walk.say: Draw an n x n grid: a row per college, a column per student. Each box is one possible offer. Every time a college makes an offer, we will write the offer's number in its box.

visual.caption: n = 3, so 9 empty boxes.

walk.look: Notice: the grid size n^2 does not depend on the preference lists at all.

walk.say: Replay the worked example. Offer 1 was a -> 1 and offer 2 was b -> 1. Number those boxes.

visual.caption: offers 1 and 2

walk.say: Offers 3 to 6 were a -> 2, then c -> 2, c -> 1, c -> 3. Number those boxes too. The run stopped after 6 offers.

visual.caption: all 6 offers of the run

walk.say: Why can a box never be used twice? By F2, each college walks along its own list in order and never goes back. c's offers went 2, then 1, then 3: exactly c's list, each box once.

visual.caption: c follows its list 2 > 1 > 3, never repeating.

walk.look: Notice: the arrows follow c's preference list, not left to right.

walk.say: So every offer fills a NEW box, and there are only n^2 boxes. The algorithm must stop after at most n^2 offers. Here it used 6 of the 9.

visual.caption: 6 boxes used, 3 never touched: at most n^2 offers.

walk.look: Notice: the empty boxes are offers that never had to happen.

walk.say: To make each offer O(1), build rank[s][c] once: the position of college c on student s's list. Offer 5 asked: does 1 prefer c to her b? Compare rank[1][c] = 3 with rank[1][b] = 1. No, reject.

visual.caption: Built once in O(n^2). Each 'who does she prefer?' is one comparison.

walk.look: Notice: one comparison, 3 vs 1, instead of scanning her list.

walk.say: Total: O(n^2) to build the rank table, plus at most n^2 offers at O(1) each (with a list of free colleges and a next[c] pointer). So Gale-Shapley runs in O(n^2).

visual.caption: at most n^2 offers x O(1) each + O(n^2) setup = O(n^2)

problems.why: This is a measure-of-progress argument: find a count that grows by one every step and has a ceiling. Here it is the set of offers made so far, which can never contain the same (college, student) box twice by F2, so it stops by n^2. The rank table makes each step O(1); scanning a list instead would cost O(n) per offer and O(n^3) total.
problems.tip: To prove a loop stops, name the thing that grows every step and the ceiling it cannot pass. For Gale-Shapley: new offers, at most n^2.

problems.title: A student's partners only improve (F1)
problems.problem: Show that in college-proposing Gale-Shapley, once a student gets her first offer she stays matched until the end, and each new partner is someone she prefers to the last one. Follow student 1 from the first worked example (her list: b > a > c).

visual.caption: Student 1's list. Before any offer she is free.

warmup.question: A matched student gets a new offer. List the only two things she can do.
warmup.answer: Trade up (accept, if the new college is to the left of her partner) or reject it (keep her partner). Neither option leaves her unmatched.

walk.say: Before any offers, student 1 is free. Her list is b > a > c, best first.

visual.caption: free, no offers yet

walk.say: Offer 1: a -> 1. A free student accepts any offer, so she now holds a. From this moment on she is matched.

visual.caption: after offer 1: holds a

walk.say: Offer 2: b -> 1. b is to the left of a, so she trades up. She drops a and takes b in the same moment, so she is never free in between.

visual.caption: after offer 2: holds b

walk.look: Notice: the pointer jumped LEFT, to someone better.

walk.say: Offer 5: c -> 1. c is to the right of b, so she rejects it and keeps b. A rejection never changes her partner.

visual.caption: after offer 5: still holds b

walk.say: Line up who she holds after every offer of the run. Once she has a partner, the row never goes back to free, and each change is a step up her list.

visual.caption: after offer 0, 1, 2, ..., 6

walk.look: Notice: free, then a, then b forever. Never back to free, never down.

walk.say: The general argument: a matched student only ever trades up or rejects. Trading up swaps her partner for a better one at once; rejecting keeps her partner. So she stays matched and her partners only improve. That is F1.

visual.caption: Her partners only move left on her list.

problems.why: The algorithm gives a student only two moves once she is matched: trade up or reject. Neither makes her free, and only the first changes her partner, always to someone she ranks higher. F1 is half of every Gale-Shapley proof: it shows everyone ends matched and that the result is stable.
problems.tip: Students only trade up; colleges only move down their lists (F2). Say which fact you are using, by name, in every proof.

problems.title: Prove the Gale-Shapley matching is stable
problems.problem: Prove that the matching M produced by college-proposing Gale-Shapley has no unstable pair. You may use F1 (once a student is matched she stays matched, and her partner only improves) and F2 (each college offers in order of its list, never repeating).

visual.caption: Suppose c and s would both rather be together.

warmup.question: By F1, a student's partner only improves. Student s held college x at some moment, and she ends the algorithm with y. Which does she like at least as much?
warmup.answer: y. Her partner can only improve after she holds x, so her final partner y is x or someone she ranks above x.

walk.say: 'No unstable pair' says something never happens, so prove it by contradiction. Suppose (c, s) is unstable in M: c is matched to s', and s is matched to c'.

visual.caption: Assume the bad pair exists.

walk.look: Notice: the teal lines are M. The dashed line is the pair we will show can't exist.

walk.say: Unpack the definition into four facts. (1) c is matched to s'. (2) s is matched to c'. (3) c prefers s to s'. (4) s prefers c to c'.

visual.caption: Facts 3 and 4, written on the lists.

walk.look: Notice: s comes before s' on c's list, and c before c' on s's list.

walk.say: Did c ever offer to s? c ended with s', so c offered to s'. By F2, c offers in list order, and s is before s' on its list. So c offered to s first.

visual.caption: c reached s before it ever reached s'.

walk.say: Yet c did not end with s, so at some moment s turned c down: she rejected it, or accepted and later dropped it. Either way she then held some college c* that she likes more than c.

visual.caption: Both cases end the same way: s holds some c* above c.

walk.look: Notice: both cases (rejected now, or dropped later) lead to the same picture.

walk.say: Carry that forward with F1: after holding c*, her partner only improves until the end. So her final partner c' is c* or better, and she prefers c' to c.

visual.caption: On s's list: c' is at or above c*, and c* is above c.

walk.say: That clashes with fact 4, which says s prefers c to c'. Both can't be true, so our assumption was false.

visual.caption: Opposite orders on the same list: contradiction.

walk.look: Notice: the two rows put c and c' in opposite orders.

walk.say: Conclusion: no unstable pair can exist in M, so the Gale-Shapley matching is stable.

visual.caption: M has no unstable pair: M is stable.

problems.why: The proof never looks at a specific instance. It uses only the two rules the algorithm follows: colleges go down their lists (F2) and students only trade up (F1). Graders look for the four facts named, F2 used to show c offered to s, both cases (rejected, or accepted then dropped), F1 carried to the end, and the contradiction stated.
problems.tip: Write the four facts on their own numbered lines before arguing. Half the points are for unpacking the definition correctly.

practice.problem: Run college-proposing Gale-Shapley (the alphabetically first free college offers next). Colleges a: 3 > 1 > 2, b: 1 > 3 > 2, c: 3 > 1 > 2. Students 1: a > c > b, 2: a > b > c, 3: b > c > a. List every offer and give the final matching.

visual.caption: Draw each offer as an arrow, number it, and cross it out if she says no.

practice.hint: Start with a's top choice. Each time a student trades up, the college she drops becomes the first free college again, so check who is free before every offer.
practice.answer: a -> 3 (accepted). b -> 1 (accepted). c -> 3: her list is b > c > a, so c beats a and she trades up; a is free. a -> 1: her list is a > c > b, so a beats b and she trades up; b is free. b -> 3: she ranks b first, so she trades up from c; c is free. c -> 1: she holds a, whom she ranks first, so she rejects c. c -> 2 (accepted). 7 offers. Matching: {(a, 1), (b, 3), (c, 2)}. Stable: a and b hold their first choices, and c's better options 3 and 1 each prefer their partners.

practice.problem: Colleges a: 2 > 1 > 3, b: 1 > 2 > 3, c: 1 > 3 > 2. Students 1: a > c > b, 2: b > a > c, 3: a > b > c. Find every unstable pair in M = {(a, 2), (b, 1), (c, 3)}. Is M stable?

visual.caption: Partners are in brackets. Test only names left of a college's bracket.

practice.hint: Two colleges already hold their first choice, so skip them. For the third, test each student it prefers: is that college left of HER bracket?
practice.answer: Only (c, 1), so M is not stable. a holds 2 and b holds 1, their first choices, so neither can be in an unstable pair. c holds 3 and its list is 1 > [3] > 2, so test only student 1: her list is a > c > [b], so she prefers c to b. Both want it: (c, 1) is unstable. (c, 2) is never tested because c prefers its 3 to 2 (and 2 ranks c last anyway).

practice.problem: Four colleges all rank 1 > 2 > 3 > 4, and four students all rank a > b > c > d. Run college-proposing Gale-Shapley and count the offers. Compare the count with n^2, and explain why no run with n = 4 could ever make more than n^2 offers.

visual.caption: Number each box in the order the offers happen.

practice.hint: Everyone wants student 1, and she likes a best. Count how many students each college has to try before one keeps it.
practice.answer: a: 1 offer (to 1, kept). b: 2 offers (1 rejects, 2 accepts). c: 3 offers. d: 4 offers. Total 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 offers, which is at most n^2 = 16. Matching {(a, 1), (b, 2), (c, 3), (d, 4)}. No run can exceed 16 because by F2 each offer is a new (college, student) pair, and there are only 4 x 4 = 16 pairs.

practice.problem: Show that in college-proposing Gale-Shapley, a college's sequence of partners only gets worse. Use college a from the first worked example (list 1 > 2 > 3) as a picture, then give the general argument.

visual.caption: Mark a's partner after each of its offers.

practice.hint: When does a college change partners, and where on its list does it look next?
practice.answer: In the example, a held 1, was dropped when 1 traded up to b, then offered to 2 and held 2: its partner went from 1 to 2, down its list. In general: by F2 a college offers in list order and never goes back. It changes partners only after being dropped, and then offers to the next student on its list, who ranks below everyone it has already tried. So each new partner ranks below the previous one.

practice.problem: Prove that in college-proposing Gale-Shapley no college is rejected by every student. (Equivalently: the algorithm ends with everyone matched.)

visual.caption: Suppose c is rejected by all 3. Who are the students holding?

practice.hint: A student only rejects when she already holds a college. What does F1 say about her after that? Then count students and colleges.
practice.answer: Suppose college c is rejected by all n students. A student rejects c only when she already holds a college, and by F1 she stays matched forever after. So after c's last offer, all n students are matched. But c is unmatched, so they are matched to the other n - 1 colleges, and each college holds at most one student. n students cannot fit into n - 1 colleges, a contradiction. So every college ends matched.

intro.big_idea: We judge an algorithm by how its running time grows as the input gets bigger, and we ignore constant factors. Big-O is shorthand for 'grows no faster than'.
intro.picture_this: Two ways to walk home: one adds a minute per block, the other doubles your time every block. On a short trip both are fine; on a long trip only one gets you home tonight.
you_know_it_when: You're asked 'how fast is it?' or 'which is bigger for large n?'
Loops inside loops, or a variable that doubles or halves
Notation like O(...), Theta(...), 'running time', 'growth rate'

visual.caption: Same small start, very different futures. The steeper curves win in the long run.

problems.title: Running time of a doubling loop
problems.problem: What is the running time of: for i = 1 to n: { j = 1; while j < n: j = 2 * j }? Trace the inner loop with n = 16 first.

visual.caption: Inner loop, n = 16: j starts at 1 and must reach 16.

warmup.question: Start at 1 and keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, ... How many doublings does it take to reach 8? To reach 1024?
warmup.answer: 3 doublings reach 8 (1, 2, 4, 8), and 10 reach 1024. The count is log2 of the target: log2 8 = 3, log2 1024 = 10.

walk.say: Focus on the inner loop first, with n = 16. j starts at 1. The test 1 < 16 is true, so the body runs.

visual.caption: start: j = 1

walk.look: Notice: j has a long way to go, but it travels by doubling.

walk.say: Iteration 1: j = 2 * 1 = 2. Still less than 16, so keep going.

visual.caption: after iteration 1: j = 2

walk.say: Iterations 2 and 3: j becomes 4, then 8. Each hop is twice as long as the last one.

visual.caption: after iteration 3: j = 8

walk.look: Notice: the hops get longer, so few hops cover a long distance.

walk.say: Iteration 4: j becomes 16. Now the test 16 < 16 is false, so the inner loop stops. That is 4 iterations, and log2 16 = 4.

visual.caption: j = 16: 4 hops, so log2 16 = 4 iterations

walk.say: In general, after k doublings j = 2^k, and the loop stops once 2^k >= n, that is after about log2 n iterations. The inner loop doesn't use i at all.

visual.caption: j = 2^k after k doublings; stop when 2^k >= n.

walk.say: The outer loop runs n times, and every pass runs the full inner loop of log2 n iterations. Independent loops multiply: n x log2 n. For n = 16 that is 16 x 4 = 64.

visual.caption: i = 1, 2, 3, ..., 16: each pass costs log2 16 = 4.

walk.say: Answer: the running time is Theta(n log n).

visual.caption: outer count x inner count

problems.why: When a loop variable multiplies by a constant each step, it reaches n after a logarithmic number of steps. When the inner loop's length doesn't depend on the outer variable, every pass costs the same, so you multiply the two counts.
problems.tip: A loop variable that doubles or halves means log n. One that goes up by 1 means n. Trace n = 16 to check yourself.

problems.title: Order functions by growth rate
problems.problem: Sort from slowest-growing to fastest: n^2, n log n, 2^n, (log n)^10, n^1.01, 2^(log2 n).

visual.caption: Six functions, six empty steps.

warmup.question: For large n, which is bigger: n^10 or 2^n? And which is bigger: n or (log n)^5?
warmup.answer: 2^n: exponentials beat every polynomial eventually. n: any power of n beats any power of log n eventually.

walk.say: Simplify before comparing. 2^(log2 n) = n, because 2 to the log2 n undoes the log. Now the pool is all familiar shapes.

visual.caption: 2^(log2 n) is just n.

walk.look: Notice: the chip now reads n, not 2^(log2 n).

walk.say: Bottom step: (log n)^10. Logs lose to every positive power of n, even raised to the 10th power.

visual.caption: logs lose to every power of n

walk.say: Next, n and then n log n. n log n is n times something that keeps growing, so it pulls ahead of n.

visual.caption: n < n log n

walk.say: n log n vs n^1.01: cancel the shared n. That leaves log n vs n^0.01. A tiny power still beats a log, so n log n < n^1.01.

visual.caption: cancel n: log n < n^0.01

walk.look: Notice: n^1.01 looks like n, but its extra n^0.01 eventually beats log n.

walk.say: n^1.01 < n^2, since the smaller power loses. Then 2^n tops everything: exponentials beat every polynomial.

visual.caption: smaller powers lose; exponentials win

walk.say: Answer: (log n)^10 < 2^(log2 n) = n < n log n < n^1.01 < n^2 < 2^n.

visual.caption: Final order, slowest to fastest.

problems.why: Three rules settle almost every comparison: logs lose to polynomials, smaller powers lose to bigger powers, and polynomials lose to exponentials. Simplify expressions like 2^(log n) first, and cancel shared factors before comparing.
problems.tip: When two terms share a factor, cancel it: n log n vs n^1.01 is really log n vs n^0.01.

problems.title: Prove a big-O bound
problems.problem: Prove that 3n^2 + 10n + 5 = O(n^2).

visual.caption: T(n) sits above plain n^2. Find a multiple of n^2 that stays above it.

warmup.question: Suppose n >= 1. Is 4n <= 4n^2? Is 7 <= 7n^2?
warmup.answer: Yes to both. When n >= 1 we have 1 <= n <= n^2, so multiplying by 4 or 7 keeps the order.

walk.say: Name the goal: find constants c > 0 and n0 so that 3n^2 + 10n + 5 <= c n^2 for every n >= n0. With c = 1 it clearly fails, so c must be bigger.

visual.caption: c = 1 is too small.

walk.look: Notice: the pink T(n) is above the dashed n^2 everywhere.

walk.say: Keep 3n^2: it is already a multiple of n^2. Raise 10n to the top power: for n >= 1, n <= n^2, so 10n <= 10n^2.
walk.look: Notice: the 10n^2 row is never smaller than the 10n row.

walk.say: Raise the constant too: for n >= 1, 1 <= n^2, so 5 <= 5n^2.

visual.caption: For n >= 1: 5 <= 5n^2 too.

walk.say: Add the pieces: 3n^2 + 10n + 5 <= 3n^2 + 10n^2 + 5n^2 = 18n^2 for all n >= 1. Add the coefficients to get c.

visual.caption: From n = 1 on, 18n^2 is a ceiling.

walk.say: Spot check a few values. At n = 1 both sides are 18 (equal is fine). At n = 2, 37 <= 72. At n = 3, 62 <= 162.

visual.caption: The ceiling holds; at n = 1 it just touches.

walk.look: Notice: n = 1 is exactly tight, which is why n0 can't be smaller.

walk.say: State the constants: c = 18 and n0 = 1. So 3n^2 + 10n + 5 is O(n^2).

visual.caption: Done: both constants named.

problems.why: Big-O means 'at most a constant times f(n), once n is large enough'. For an upper bound you may make the right side bigger, so once n >= 1 you raise every lower-order term to the top power and add the coefficients.
problems.tip: You don't need the smallest c, just one that works. Finish by naming both c and n0.

problems.title: Prove a big-Omega bound
problems.problem: Prove from the definition that T(n) = n^2 - 6n is Omega(n^2).

visual.caption: T(n) always sits below n^2. We need a FLOOR c n^2 under it.

warmup.question: You want to show T(n) >= something. May you drop a positive term from T(n)? May you drop a negative term?
warmup.answer: Dropping a positive term is safe: T only gets smaller. Dropping a negative term is not: it makes T bigger, which can break a lower bound.

walk.say: Name the goal: find c > 0 and n0 with n^2 - 6n >= c n^2 for all n >= n0. The inequality points the other way now: this is a floor, not a ceiling.

visual.caption: c = 1 fails: T(n) is always below n^2.

walk.look: Notice: the pink curve never reaches the dashed n^2, so c must be below 1.

walk.say: Pick c = 1/2. It must be below the top coefficient 1, to leave room to absorb the -6n.

visual.caption: Try the floor n^2/2.

walk.say: Solve for where it holds: n^2 - 6n >= n^2/2 means n^2/2 >= 6n, which means n >= 12. Dividing by n is safe because n > 0.

visual.caption: n^2 - 6n >= n^2/2 exactly when n >= 12.

walk.say: Spot check. n = 10: 40 < 50, fails (allowed, it's below n0). n = 12: 72 = 72, just holds. n = 14: 112 >= 98, holds.

visual.caption: fails, ties, holds

walk.look: Notice: the definition lets small n fail. That's what n0 is for.

walk.say: State the constants: c = 1/2 and n0 = 12. So n^2 - 6n is Omega(n^2).

visual.caption: From n = 12 on, the floor stays under T(n).

problems.why: For a lower bound you may only make the right side SMALLER: drop positive terms, or show the negative terms are small next to the main term. n0 is exactly the point where the negative term stops mattering.
problems.tip: Choose c a bit below the leading coefficient (half is easy), then solve for n0 instead of guessing it.

problems.title: Prove Theta with both directions
problems.problem: Prove that T(n) = 2n^2 + 10n is Theta(n^2).

visual.caption: Trap T(n) between two multiples of n^2.

warmup.question: Fill in: T is Theta(f) means T is ____(f) AND T is ____(f).
warmup.answer: T is O(f) and Omega(f): a ceiling and a floor, both multiples of the same f.

walk.say: Say the plan: Theta means both O(n^2) and Omega(n^2), so there are two small proofs. One direction alone doesn't earn Theta.

visual.caption: We need a ceiling and a floor.

walk.say: Upper bound: for n >= 1, 10n <= 10n^2, so T(n) <= 2n^2 + 10n^2 = 12n^2. Constants c = 12, n0 = 1.

visual.caption: ceiling: 12n^2

walk.look: Notice: raising 10n to 10n^2 is the move for a ceiling.

walk.say: Lower bound: 10n is positive, so throw it away. T(n) >= 2n^2. Constants c = 2, n0 = 1.

visual.caption: floor: 2n^2

walk.look: Notice: dropping a positive term is the move for a floor.

visual.caption: T(n) sits between the other two rows.

walk.say: Conclude: 2n^2 <= T(n) <= 12n^2 for all n >= 1, so T(n) is Theta(n^2). The two directions used different c's, and that's fine.

visual.caption: Squeezed: Theta(n^2).

problems.why: Theta traps T(n) between two multiples of the same function. Each direction gets its own c and n0; they don't have to match. Upper bounds raise lower terms to the top power; lower bounds throw positive terms away.
problems.tip: Write 'Upper:' and 'Lower:' as two labeled lines, each ending with its own c and n0.

problems.title: Count loops: does the inner loop depend on the outer one?
problems.problem: Give a tight bound for each. (A) i = n; while i > 1: { for j = 1 to n: body }; i = i / 2. (B) i = n; while i > 1: { for j = 1 to i: body }; i = i / 2. (C) for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to i: for k = 1 to 3: body.

visual.caption: n = 16: i = 16, 8, 4, 2. Write each pass's inner-loop count.

warmup.question: With n = 4, how many times does body run in: for i = 1 to 4: for j = 1 to i: body?
warmup.answer: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The inner loop's length depends on i, so you add the passes instead of multiplying.

walk.say: (A) with n = 16: i takes 16, 8, 4, 2, then stops at 1. That's 4 passes, and each pass runs the full j-loop of 16. Total 4 x 16 = 64.

visual.caption: every pass costs n

walk.look: Notice: every box is the same, 16. The inner loop ignores i.

walk.say: (A) in general: halving i gives about log n passes, each costing n. The loops are independent, so multiply: Theta(n log n).

visual.caption: (A) = Theta(n log n)

walk.say: (B) with n = 16: same 4 passes, but now the j-loop runs to i, so the passes cost 16, 8, 4, 2. Add them: 30.

visual.caption: Same passes, shrinking costs.

walk.look: Notice: (B)'s boxes halve. The inner loop depends on i.

walk.say: (B) in general: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... is less than 2n, and at least n from the first pass alone. So (B) is Theta(n), not n log n.

visual.caption: a halving sum: the first term dominates

walk.say: (C) with n = 4: row i runs j = 1..i, and each (i, j) runs k three times. Shade the triangle: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 cells, x 3 = 30.

visual.caption: n = 4: 10 shaded cells x 3 = 30

walk.look: Notice: the shaded cells form a triangle, about half the square.

walk.say: (C) in general: 3(1 + 2 + ... + n) = 3n(n + 1)/2. The k-loop has fixed length 3, so it is only a constant factor: Theta(n^2).

visual.caption: about n^2/2 cells x 3 = Theta(n^2)

walk.say: Answer: (A) Theta(n log n), (B) Theta(n), (C) Theta(n^2). (A) and (B) look alike, but (B)'s inner loop depends on i, so you add a shrinking sum.

visual.caption: tight bounds

problems.why: Independent nested loops multiply. Dependent loops sum, so write the sum out. A loop of fixed length (k = 1 to 3) is only a constant factor and adds no power of n. A variable that doubles or halves gives log n passes.
problems.tip: Always ask: does the inner loop's length depend on the outer variable? If yes, write the sum; if no, multiply.

problems.title: Prove something is NOT big-O
problems.problem: Prove that n sqrt(n) is not O(n).

visual.caption: One try, c = 5. We must beat EVERY c.

warmup.question: Is there a constant c with n <= c for every n >= 1? Why or why not?
warmup.answer: No. Whatever c someone picks, n = c + 1 is bigger than c. A growing quantity can't stay under a fixed number.

walk.say: You can't test every c, so assume one exists and break it. Suppose there are constants c and n0 with n sqrt(n) <= c n for all n >= n0.

visual.caption: Picture c = 5, but the proof works for any c.

walk.look: Notice: the pink curve bends upward; the line doesn't.

walk.say: Divide both sides by n (positive, so the inequality keeps its direction): sqrt(n) <= c for all n >= n0.

visual.caption: Now: a growing curve vs a flat line.

walk.say: Spot the problem: the left side grows forever and the right side is a fixed number. A bigger c only moves the crossing further out.

visual.caption: sqrt(n) passes 5 at n = 25 and 8 at n = 64.

walk.look: Notice: every flat line gets crossed, at n = c^2.

walk.say: Choose n = max(n0, c^2 + 1). It is at least n0, so the assumption applies. And sqrt(n) >= sqrt(c^2 + 1) > c.
Check the example: n = 26 gives sqrt(26) = 5.10, which is more than c = 5. So sqrt(n) <= c fails at an n >= n0.

visual.caption: 5.10 > 5: the claim breaks.

walk.say: That contradicts sqrt(n) <= c for all n >= n0. So no constants c and n0 exist, and n sqrt(n) is not O(n).

visual.caption: Past c^2 the ceiling cn always breaks.

problems.why: To show 'not O(f)', assume the constants exist, simplify to 'something growing <= a constant', then pick an n big enough to break it. Using max(n0, ...) makes your n satisfy both needs at once: it's in range, and it's too big.
problems.tip: Name the n that breaks it in terms of c and n0. Graders want to see max(n0, something) written out.

problems.title: Compare growth rates by transforming both sides
problems.problem: Which grows faster, (log n)^2 or sqrt(n)? Prove it, then find where the winner takes over (try powers of 2).

visual.caption: At n = 2^10, (log n)^2 looks like the winner. Is it?

warmup.question: Let n = 2^k. Write log n, (log n)^2 and sqrt(n) in terms of k.
warmup.answer: log n = k, (log n)^2 = k^2, and sqrt(n) = 2^(k/2).

walk.say: Plug in one size first: n = 2^10 gives (log n)^2 = 100 and sqrt(n) = 32. The log side is ahead here, but big-O is about what happens eventually.

visual.caption: ahead for now

walk.look: Notice: one value can't settle growth rates. We need a proof.

walk.say: Simplify: take the square root of both sides. Now compare log n with n^(1/4). Doing the same increasing operation to both keeps the comparison honest.

visual.caption: square root of both sides

walk.say: Use the hierarchy: log n is O(n^d) for every d > 0, including d = 1/4. Logs lose to every positive power.

visual.caption: logs < powers

walk.say: Undo the root by squaring both sides: (log n)^2 is O(sqrt(n)). So sqrt(n) grows faster.

visual.caption: squaring keeps the order

walk.say: Find the takeover with n = 2^k, so (log n)^2 = k^2 and sqrt(n) = 2^(k/2). k = 10: 100 vs 32. k = 16: 256 vs 256, a tie. k = 20: 400 vs 1024.

visual.caption: tie at n = 2^16, then sqrt(n) pulls away

walk.say: Plot both against k = log n. k^2 is ahead for every n from 3 up to 2^16, they tie at k = 16, and 2^(k/2) wins from then on.

visual.caption: x-axis: k = log n

walk.look: Notice: the shaded zone is where sqrt(n) is ahead for good.

walk.say: Answer: sqrt(n) grows faster; (log n)^2 is O(sqrt(n)). The log side leads for a long while, ties at n = 2^16 = 65,536, and loses from then on.

visual.caption: (log n)^2 = O(sqrt(n))

problems.why: Big-O only cares about what happens past n0, and the eventual winner can lose for a long time. Dividing, taking roots or taking logs of both sides turns a messy comparison into one the hierarchy (logs < powers < exponentials) answers directly.
problems.tip: Plug in n = 2^k: then log n = k, and every term becomes a plain power of 2 you can compare in your head.

practice.problem: Running time of: for i = 1 to n: { j = 1; while j < n: j = 3 * j }? Trace the inner loop with n = 81, then give a tight bound.

visual.caption: Draw each hop of j for n = 81.

practice.hint: Tripling works like doubling: write the values j takes until j >= 81, count the hops, then ask whether the inner loop depends on i.
practice.answer: j takes 1, 3, 9, 27, 81: that is 4 iterations, and log3 81 = 4. In general the inner loop runs about log3 n times, independent of i, so the total is n x log3 n. log3 n = (log2 n) / (log2 3) is a constant times log n, so the running time is Theta(n log n). The base of the log never matters.

practice.problem: Sort from slowest to fastest: n^3, 3^n, n^2 log n, sqrt(n), log(n!), 2^n.
practice.answer: sqrt(n) < log(n!) < n^2 log n < n^3 < 2^n < 3^n. The key fact is log(n!) = Theta(n log n), from Stirling or from n! <= n^n and n! >= (n/2)^(n/2).
practice.hint: Rewrite log(n!) first: it is Theta(n log n). Then place the logs and roots, then the polynomials by power, then the exponentials by base.

practice.problem: Prove 5n^3 + 2n + 7 = O(n^3).

visual.caption: Pick a c so that c times n^3 sits above the pink curve for every n >= n0.

practice.hint: Keep 5n^3. For n >= 1, raise each smaller term to n^3, then add the coefficients.

practice.problem: Prove from the definition that n^2 - 100n is Omega(n^2).

visual.caption: Pick c, fill in both rows, and find where the floor c n^2 drops under the top row.

practice.hint: Take c = 1/2 as in the worked example. Then solve n^2 - 100n >= n^2/2 for n.
practice.answer: Take c = 1/2. n^2 - 100n >= n^2/2 means n^2/2 >= 100n, which means n >= 200 (dividing by n > 0). So for all n >= 200, n^2 - 100n >= n^2/2. Constants: c = 1/2, n0 = 200. Table with c = 1/2: n = 100: 0 vs 5,000 (fails); 150: 7,500 vs 11,250 (fails); 200: 20,000 vs 20,000 (just holds); 250: 37,500 vs 31,250 (holds).

practice.problem: Prove that 5n^3 - 2n^2 + 7 is Theta(n^3) by giving both an upper and a lower bound with explicit constants.
practice.answer: Upper: for n >= 1, -2n^2 <= 0 and 7 <= 7n^3, so the expression is at most 5n^3 + 7n^3 = 12n^3 (c = 12, n0 = 1). Lower: for n >= 1, 2n^2 <= 2n^3 and +7 > 0, so the expression is at least 5n^3 - 2n^3 = 3n^3 (c = 3, n0 = 1). Together: Theta(n^3).

visual.caption: Find a ceiling c1 n^3 above and a floor c2 n^3 below, from some n0 on.

practice.hint: Upper: drop the negative -2n^2 and raise 7 to 7n^3. Lower: drop the +7, and for n >= 1 replace -2n^2 by the larger loss -2n^3.

practice.problem: Give the exact count and a tight bound. (a) for i = 1 to n: for j = i to n: body. (b) for i = 1 to n: { print X; if i == 1: for j = 1 to n: print Y }. (c) for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to 3: body. For (a), also show Omega(n^2) without the exact formula.
practice.answer: (a) n + (n - 1) + ... + 1 = n(n + 1)/2, Theta(n^2); with n = 5 that is 15 shaded cells. Lower bound trick: the iterations with i <= n/2 and j >= n/2 alone number at least (n/2)(n/2) = n^2/4, so Omega(n^2). (b) n X's plus n Y's (the inner loop runs only once, when i == 1) = 2n, Theta(n). (c) 3n, Theta(n): a fixed-length inner loop is a constant factor.

visual.caption: For (a) with n = 5: shade every (i, j) the loops visit, then count.

practice.hint: For each part, ask whether the inner loop depends on i. Count n = 5 by hand for (a); for (b), how many values of i make the inner loop run?

practice.problem: Prove that (a) n log n is not O(n), and (b) 3n^2 + 7 is not O(n).
practice.answer: (a) Suppose n log n <= c n for all n >= n0. Divide by n: log n <= c. Take n = max(n0, 2^(c + 1)); then log n >= c + 1 > c. Contradiction. (b) Suppose 3n^2 + 7 <= c n for all n >= n0. Then 3n^2 <= c n, so 3n <= c. Take n = max(n0, c) + 1; then 3n > c. Contradiction.

visual.caption: Try c = 4: where does n log n pass 4n? Then do it for any c.

practice.hint: Assume the constants exist and divide both sides by n. What is left is a growing thing <= c. Pick n = max(n0, something) that breaks it.

practice.problem: Which grows faster, n (log n)^3 or n^(4/3)? Prove it by transforming both sides. Then fill in the table (with n = 2^k) to see roughly where the winner takes over.

visual.caption: After dividing both sides by n. With n = 2^k: k^3 vs 2^(k/3).

practice.hint: Both sides share a factor of n: divide it out first. Then take a cube root, and compare a log with a small power.
practice.answer: Divide both by n: (log n)^3 vs n^(1/3). Take cube roots: log n vs n^(1/9). By the hierarchy, log n is O(n^(1/9)), so n (log n)^3 is O(n^(4/3)): n^(4/3) grows faster. Table: k = 9: 729 vs 8; k = 27: 19,683 vs 512; k = 54: 157,464 vs 262,144. The log side leads until about n = 2^52 (from k = 52 on, 2^(k/3) > k^3), then n^(4/3) wins for good.

intro.big_idea: A graph is dots (nodes) joined by lines (edges). Breadth-first search explores it in rings: first everything one step away, then two steps away, and so on.
intro.picture_this: Ripples from a pebble in a pond: the first ring is your friends, the next ring is friends of friends.
you_know_it_when: Things connected to other things: roads, friendships, prerequisites, links
Questions like 'can I get from s to t?', 'how many groups?', 'what order?'
Anything you could sketch as dots and arrows

visual.caption: BFS from s: each layer is one more step away.

problems.title: BFS layers, tree edges and non-tree edges
problems.problem: Graph with edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 3-4, 4-5, 5-6, 5-7, 6-7. Run BFS from 1 with a queue (neighbors in increasing order). Give the layers, the BFS tree edges, the non-tree edges with their endpoints' layers, and the distance from 1 to 7.

visual.caption: A square 1-2-4-3, the edge 4-5, and a triangle 5-6-7. n = 7, m = 8.

warmup.question: Graph with edges 1-2, 1-3, 3-4. Which nodes are exactly one edge from 1? Which are two edges away?
warmup.answer: One away: 2 and 3, so they form layer 1. Two away: 4, found from 3, so it is layer 2. BFS is just these rings, one step at a time.

walk.say: Start: node 1 goes in the queue on its own. It is layer 0, distance 0 from itself.

visual.caption: queue: 1

walk.look: Notice: nothing else is colored yet. A node gets a color (a layer) the moment it is first found.

walk.say: Explore 1: its neighbors 2 and 3 are both new. They join the back of the queue and form layer 1. The edges 1-2 and 1-3 found them, so they are tree edges.

visual.caption: queue: 2, 3

walk.say: Explore 2: neighbor 1 is already found, so cross it off. Neighbor 4 is new: it joins the queue in layer 2, and 2-4 is a tree edge.

visual.caption: queue: 3, 4

walk.say: Explore 3: neighbors 1 and 4 are both already found. Nothing new. The edge 3-4 discovered nobody, so it is a non-tree edge.

visual.caption: queue: 4

walk.look: Notice: 3-4 runs from layer 1 to layer 2. 2 got to 4 first, but 4's layer is the same either way.

walk.say: Explore 4: neighbors 2 and 3 are old, 5 is new. 5 is layer 3, and 4-5 is a tree edge.

visual.caption: queue: 5

walk.say: Explore 5: 4 is old, 6 and 7 are new. They form layer 4, with tree edges 5-6 and 5-7.

visual.caption: queue: 6, 7

walk.say: Explore 6, then 7: each only sees nodes already found. So 6-7 is a non-tree edge, with both ends in layer 4. The queue is empty, so BFS stops.

visual.caption: queue: empty

walk.say: Answer. Layers L0 = {1}, L1 = {2, 3}, L2 = {4}, L3 = {5}, L4 = {6, 7}. Tree edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 4-5, 5-6, 5-7 (6 = n - 1). Non-tree edges 3-4 (L1 to L2) and 6-7 (L4 to L4). 7 is in L4, so its distance from 1 is 4.

visual.caption: 6 tree + 2 non-tree = 8 = m. Nothing is missing.

walk.look: Notice: neither dashed edge skips a layer. One joins neighboring layers, the other stays inside one.

problems.why: Layer i is exactly the set of nodes at distance i from the start. Every edge joins nodes in the same layer or adjacent layers, never farther apart. Which node 'claims' a newly found node depends on the order (2 found 4, not 3), but the layers themselves never do.
problems.tip: Keep a running queue column as you go. Each node enters the queue exactly once, so cross it off the moment it's found.

problems.title: Recursive DFS and the ancestor rule
problems.problem: Edges a-b, a-d, b-c, b-e, c-e, d-e, e-f. Run recursive DFS from a with neighbors in alphabetical order. Keep the call stack on paper. Give the explored order, tree edges and non-tree edges, and check that every non-tree edge joins a node to one of its ancestors.

visual.caption: n = 6, m = 7. DFS goes as deep as it can before it backs up.

warmup.question: Edges x-y, y-z, x-z. Run DFS from x, neighbors in alphabetical order. Which node is reached second, and which third? Which edge never discovers anything?
warmup.answer: x calls y first, and y goes deeper to z before x ever looks at z. Order x, y, z. Edge x-z discovers nothing: it is the non-tree edge, and x is z's ancestor.

walk.say: DFS(a) looks at its first neighbor, b. It is new, so a pauses and calls DFS(b). Write the call stack: a b.

visual.caption: stack: a b

walk.look: Notice: yellow nodes are paused calls on the stack. The bold one is running right now.

walk.say: DFS(b): a is already explored, so skip it. c is new: pause b and call DFS(c). Stack: a b c.

visual.caption: stack: a b c

walk.say: DFS(c): b is explored, e is new. Call DFS(e). Stack: a b c e. We are four calls deep and haven't backed up once.

visual.caption: stack: a b c e

walk.say: DFS(e): b and c are explored, so b-e is a non-tree edge. d is new: call DFS(d). DFS(d) sees a and e explored (a-d is non-tree) and returns. The stack is back to a b c e.

visual.caption: stack: a b c e

walk.look: Notice: d is finished (teal), and e picks up exactly where it paused. That is all backtracking is.

walk.say: DFS(e) resumes at its next neighbor, f: new, so call DFS(f). f has nothing new and returns. Then e, c, b and a each find nothing new and return. The stack is empty.

visual.caption: stack: empty

walk.say: Answer. Order a, b, c, e, d, f. Tree edges a-b, b-c, c-e, e-d, e-f (5 = n - 1). Non-tree edges a-d and b-e (5 + 2 = 7 = m). Redraw by depth: a is d's ancestor and b is e's ancestor, so both run straight up a branch.

visual.caption: Drawn by depth. Both dashed edges point back up to an ancestor.

walk.look: Notice: no dashed edge runs sideways between two branches. That's the DFS ancestor rule.

problems.why: Claim: if (x, y) is a non-tree edge and x is explored first, y is a descendant of x. When DFS(x) finally looks at edge (x, y), y must already be explored (otherwise y would become x's child). y wasn't explored when DFS(x) started, so it was explored inside DFS(x)'s recursion: a descendant. So DFS non-tree edges never run sideways between branches.
problems.tip: When a call returns, write the stack again. 'Backtracking' is just the paused call below resuming at its next neighbor.

problems.title: Count connected components
problems.problem: Give an O(m + n) algorithm to count the connected components of an undirected graph. Trace it on nodes 1 to 7 with edges 1-2, 2-3, 1-3, 4-5, 5-6.

visual.caption: 7 nodes, 5 edges. Node 7 has no edges at all.

warmup.question: Nodes a, b, c, d and a single edge a-b. How many connected components are there? List them.
warmup.answer: Three: {a, b}, {c} and {d}. A node with no edges is a whole component by itself.

walk.say: Mark every node unexplored and set count = 0. Then scan the nodes in order 1, 2, 3, ... and ask one question at each: is it unexplored?

visual.caption: count = 0

walk.say: Node 1 is unexplored, so count = 1. BFS from 1 reaches 1, 2 and 3 and marks all three. That one search found a whole component.

visual.caption: count = 1

walk.look: Notice: one search colors exactly one component, no more and no less.

walk.say: Nodes 2 and 3 are already marked, so skip them. Node 4 is unexplored: count = 2, and BFS from 4 marks 4, 5, 6.

visual.caption: count = 2

walk.say: Skip 5 and 6. Node 7 is unexplored: count = 3. BFS from 7 reaches only 7, since it has no edges. The scan ends with count = 3.

visual.caption: count = 3

walk.look: Notice: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. Every node landed in exactly one component.

walk.say: Cost: each BFS only touches its own component's nodes and adjacency lists, and no node is searched twice. Added up that's every node once and 2m list entries: O(m + n). Answer: 3 components. The algorithm: for each node, if unexplored, add 1 to count and search from it.

visual.caption: The searches split the work: 7 = n nodes and 10 = 2m list entries in total.

walk.look: Notice: node 7 costs 1 even with no edges. That's why the bound keeps the n.

problems.why: Each BFS finds exactly one whole component, and a component is only started once because its nodes are marked afterwards. Every node and edge is handled a constant number of times across all the searches, so the total is O(m + n).
problems.tip: 'For each node, if it's unvisited, search from it' is the template for lots of graph problems.

problems.title: Topological order of a DAG
problems.problem: Find a topological order for the DAG with edges a->b, a->c, b->d, c->d, d->e. When more than one node is ready, take the first alphabetically.

visual.caption: An edge u -> v means u must come before v.

warmup.question: Edges x->y and y->z. Which node has no incoming edges, so it can go first? What order comes out?
warmup.answer: x: nothing points into it. Once x is placed, y has no incoming edges left, and then z. Order x, y, z.

walk.say: Count each node's incoming edges: a 0, b 1, c 1, d 2, e 1. A node with count 0 has nothing that must come before it, so it is ready. Only a is ready.
walk.look: Notice: the yellow tags are the counts. Yellow fill means ready to place.

walk.say: Place a as #1 and delete its edges. b and c each drop to 0, so both are ready now.
Two nodes are ready, so take the first alphabetically: place b as #2. Its edge b->d goes away, and d drops to 1.
walk.look: Notice: d isn't ready yet. It still waits on c.

walk.say: Place c as #3. d drops to 0, so d is ready.
Place d as #4. e drops to 0. Place e as #5. Every node got placed, which also proves there was no cycle.
Answer: a, b, c, d, e. Check by lining them up: every arrow points to the right. (a, c, b, d, e also works; those are the only two.)

visual.caption: All five arrows point forward.

walk.look: Notice: a single arrow pointing left would mean the order is wrong.

problems.why: Every DAG has a node with no incoming edges, and deleting it leaves a DAG, so the process never gets stuck. Track each node's count of incoming edges and a list of nodes at zero, and the whole thing runs in O(m + n).
problems.tip: Keep an 'incoming edges' count on each node; the moment a count hits 0, that node is ready to go.

problems.title: Test whether a graph is bipartite
problems.problem: Use BFS to decide whether the 5-cycle 1-2-3-4-5-1 is bipartite. If it isn't, name an odd cycle.

visual.caption: Bipartite means: 2 colors, every edge joins different colors.

warmup.question: Try to color a triangle a-b-c with two colors so that every edge joins different colors. What happens?
warmup.answer: Color a pink and b blue. c touches both, so it can't be either color. An odd cycle always gets stuck like this.

walk.say: Run plain BFS from 1. Layer 0 is just {1}. Color even layers pink and odd layers blue.
Layer 1 = the neighbors of 1 = {2, 5}. They're odd, so blue.
Layer 2 = new neighbors of 2 and 5: 2 finds 3, and 5 finds 4. So L2 = {3, 4}, colored pink.
walk.look: Notice: every node now has a color. The test only checks the edges.

walk.say: Check every edge for two ends in the same layer. 1-2 and 1-5 join L0 and L1. 2-3 and 5-4 join L1 and L2. But 3-4 has both ends in L2: both pink. That one edge breaks the 2-coloring.
walk.look: Notice: one same-layer edge is enough for 'not bipartite'.

walk.say: Find the odd cycle: walk up from 3 and 4 until the paths meet. 3, 2, 1 and 4, 5, 1 meet at 1 (layer 0). The cycle is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1, of length 2(2 - 0) + 1 = 5.

visual.caption: Two equal walks down, plus one edge across: always odd.

walk.say: Answer: not bipartite. The odd cycle is the 5-cycle itself: going around, the colors must alternate, and with 5 nodes the last one has no color left.

visual.caption: 4 touches pink 3 and blue 5.

walk.look: Notice: any odd cycle (triangle, 5-cycle, ...) is an instant no.

problems.why: In BFS every edge joins nodes in the same layer or adjacent layers. If no edge stays inside a layer, the even/odd coloring works. If one does, that edge plus the two BFS paths back to their common ancestor forms an odd cycle, and a graph with an odd cycle can't be 2-colored. It runs in O(m + n).
problems.tip: Any odd-length cycle makes a graph non-bipartite, so a triangle or a 5-cycle is an instant 'no'.

problems.title: BFS tree or DFS tree?
problems.problem: Each row is a rooted tree plus one dashed non-tree edge from the same graph. Which traversal could have built it? (1) r has children x, y; x has child z; dashed z-y. (2) Path r, x, y; dashed r-y. (3) r has children x, y; dashed x-y.

warmup.question: In a BFS tree from r, node u is at depth 1 and node w is at depth 3. Could u-w be an edge of the graph?
warmup.answer: No. If u-w were an edge, exploring u would have found w, putting w at depth 2 at most. BFS edges never skip a layer.

walk.say: Two tests. BFS: a non-tree edge joins depths that differ by at most 1. DFS: a non-tree edge joins a node to one of its ancestors. Check each dashed edge against both.

panels.caption: BFS allows: depths differ by 0 or 1, any branches
DFS allows: straight up to an ancestor, any distance

walk.look: Notice: d0, d1, ... are depths. BFS edges may cross between branches; DFS edges may skip levels. Neither does both.

walk.say: (1) z is at depth 2 and y at depth 1: they differ by 1, so BFS is fine. But y is not z's ancestor (they're on different branches), so not DFS. DFS(z) would have found y unexplored and made y its child.

visual.caption: (1) BFS yes, DFS no

walk.say: (2) r is at depth 0 and y at depth 2: that skips a layer, so not BFS. BFS from r would have put y in layer 1, since r-y is an edge. r is y's ancestor, so DFS is fine.

visual.caption: (2) BFS no, DFS yes

walk.say: (3) x and y are siblings at depth 1: a sideways edge. Depths differ by 0, so BFS is fine. Neither is the other's ancestor, so not DFS: DFS(x) would have found y unexplored and made it x's child.

visual.caption: (3) BFS yes, DFS no

walk.say: Answer: (1) BFS, (2) DFS, (3) BFS. For full marks, say what the wrong traversal would have done differently.

problems.why: The two non-tree edge facts decide it. BFS edges can run sideways between branches but never skip a layer. DFS edges can skip many levels but never run sideways. Say what the wrong traversal would have done; that sentence earns the point.
problems.tip: Two quick questions: do the depths differ by more than 1 (then not BFS)? Is one end an ancestor of the other (if not, then not DFS)?

problems.title: Count topological orderings
problems.problem: DAG with edges s -> a, a -> b, b -> t, s -> c, c -> d, d -> t. How many topological orderings are there? List them. Must a come before d? Must a come before b?

visual.caption: Two chains between s and t.

warmup.question: A DAG has only the edges s->x and s->y. How many topological orderings does it have?
warmup.answer: Two: s, x, y and s, y, x. s must be first; there is no path between x and y, so either can go next.

walk.say: s has no incoming edges and every other node is reachable from it, so s is always first. Everything leads into t, so t is always last.
In between are two separate chains, a -> b and c -> d. Each chain keeps its own order, but no edge or path links one chain to the other.
walk.look: Notice: blue a -> b and pink c -> d never touch each other.

walk.say: Count: the middle has 4 slots. Choose which 2 of them hold a and b: C(4, 2) = 6 ways. Then a takes the earlier one and b the later; c and d fill the other two in order.
List them to check the count: six orderings, each with s first and t last.
walk.look: Notice: in every row the blues stay in order a, b and the pinks in order c, d.

walk.say: Answer: 6 orderings. Must a come before d? No: row 6 (c, d, a, b) puts d first, because there is no path between a and d. Must a come before b? Yes, in every row, because there is a path a -> b.

visual.caption: a-b has a path, so it's forced. a and d have none, so either order works.

problems.why: u must come before w in EVERY ordering exactly when there is a directed path from u to w; with no path either way, some ordering puts each one first. The C(p + q, p) shortcut only works for separate chains. For any other DAG, branch on the available sources at each step and count the leaves.
problems.tip: Before counting, mark which pairs are forced (a path exists) and which are free. Only the free pairs create choices.

problems.title: Design an O(m + n) cycle test
problems.problem: Design an O(m + n) algorithm that decides whether an undirected graph G has a cycle. Give the algorithm, a correctness proof and the running time.

visual.caption: Example to test the idea on: n = 5, m = 5.

warmup.question: A connected graph has 6 nodes and 6 edges. Must it contain a cycle?
warmup.answer: Yes. A tree on 6 nodes has exactly 5 edges. A connected graph with a 6th edge must close a loop somewhere.

walk.say: The algorithm: run BFS from each unexplored node (one search tree per component). Answer 'cycle' exactly when some edge is NOT a tree edge. On the example, BFS from 1 builds the tree 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 3-5.

visual.caption: BFS tree from 1 (4 edges = n - 1)

walk.say: Edge 4-5 discovered nobody: it is a non-tree edge. So the algorithm answers 'cycle'.

visual.caption: 1 non-tree edge left over

walk.say: Proof, part 1: a non-tree edge (x, y) means a cycle. x and y are in the same search tree, so a tree path already joins them: here 4, 2, 1, 3, 5. Adding the edge 4-5 closes it into a cycle.
walk.look: Notice: the tree path plus the one extra edge make the loop.

walk.say: Proof, part 2: if every edge is a tree edge, the edges form a forest (trees only), and trees have no cycles. Without 4-5, the same graph is just the tree.

visual.caption: all tree edges: no cycle

walk.say: Equivalent count: with k components, G is acyclic exactly when m = n - k, since a tree on n_i nodes has n_i - 1 edges.
Time, assuming adjacency lists: the searches explore each node once and scan each list once, 2m entries in all. Answer: 'cycle iff some non-tree edge', correct by parts 1 and 2, in O(m + n).

visual.caption: 10 list entries = 2m. Each is looked at once.

walk.look: Notice: the non-tree edge 4-5 appears twice, once in each end's list.

problems.why: A full-credit 'design an algorithm' answer has five parts: the algorithm, the intuition, a correctness proof (here both directions of 'cycle iff non-tree edge'), the running time, and why (count the lines; adjacency lists make 'for each neighbor' cost the degree).
problems.tip: Say 'assume adjacency lists' out loud in your answer. The O(m + n) bound depends on it.

practice.problem: Graph G (adjacency lists, visit neighbors in this order): A: B, C | B: A, D | C: A, D, E | D: B, C, F | E: C, F | F: D, E, G | G: F, H | H: G. Run BFS from A. Give the layers, the tree edges, the non-tree edges with their endpoints' layers, and the distance from A to H. Check that the degrees sum to 2m.
practice.answer: L0 = {A}, L1 = {B, C}, L2 = {D, E}, L3 = {F}, L4 = {G}, L5 = {H}. Tree edges: A-B, A-C, B-D, C-E, D-F, F-G, G-H. Non-tree edges: C-D (layers 1 and 2; B already found D) and E-F (layers 2 and 3; D already found F). Distance A to H = 5. n = 8, m = 9, degrees 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1 sum to 18 = 2m.

visual.caption: Two squares sharing C-D, with a tail F-G-H.

practice.hint: Keep a queue column. Explore A first: B and C are new, so they are layer 1. A node's layer is one more than the layer of the node that found it.

practice.problem: Graph G: A: B, C | B: A, D | C: A, D, E | D: B, C, F | E: C, F | F: D, E, G | G: F, H | H: G. Run recursive DFS from A (neighbors in this order). Give the explored order, tree edges and non-tree edges, and name the ancestor endpoint of each non-tree edge.
practice.answer: DFS(A) -> B -> D; D's first unexplored neighbor is C -> E -> F -> G -> H. Order A, B, D, C, E, F, G, H. Tree edges A-B, B-D, D-C, C-E, E-F, F-G, G-H. Non-tree edges A-C (A is C's ancestor) and D-F (D is F's ancestor).

visual.caption: Write the call stack after every call; number each node when its call starts.

practice.hint: From A, the first neighbor is B; from B, it's D. At D, look at its list in order: B is explored, so C comes next. Keep going deeper before you back up.

practice.problem: Nodes 1 to 9, edges 1-6, 6-3, 2-5, 4-8, 8-9, 4-9. (a) Run the scan-and-search algorithm, scanning 1, 2, ..., 9. Which nodes start a new search, what does each search find, and what is the final count? (b) The algorithm runs up to n searches. Why is it still O(m + n) and not O(n(m + n))?

visual.caption: Circle each component as your searches find it.

practice.hint: Node 1 is unexplored, so it starts search #1. When the scan reaches a node some earlier search already marked, skip it.
practice.answer: (a) Scan 1: new, count = 1, the search finds {1, 6, 3}. Scan 2: new, count = 2, finds {2, 5}. 3 is marked. Scan 4: new, count = 3, finds {4, 8, 9}. 5 and 6 are marked. Scan 7: new, count = 4, finds only {7}. 8 and 9 are marked. Searches start at 1, 2, 4 and 7, so there are 4 components (3 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 9 nodes). (b) A search only touches its own component, and a marked node is never searched again. So over all the searches each node is handled once and each adjacency list is scanned once (2m entries in total): O(m + n), however many searches there are.

practice.problem: Find a topological order for edges x->y, z->y, y->w, z->w, w->v.
practice.answer: Counts: x 0, z 0, y 2, w 2, v 1. Place x (y drops to 1). Place z (y drops to 0, w to 1). Place y (w drops to 0). Place w (v drops to 0). Place v. Order: x, z, y, w, v. The only other valid order is z, x, y, w, v, since x and z are the only pair with no path between them.
practice.hint: Count incoming edges first. Two nodes start at 0. Each time you place a node, subtract 1 from everything it points to.

practice.problem: Is the 6-cycle 1-2-3-4-5-6-1 plus the extra edge 1-4 bipartite? Use BFS from 1.
practice.answer: Layers: L0 = {1}, L1 = {2, 4, 6}, L2 = {3, 5} (2 finds 3, 4 finds 5). Edges 1-2, 1-4, 1-6 join L0 and L1; 2-3, 3-4, 4-5, 5-6 join L1 and L2. No edge stays inside a layer, so yes, it is bipartite: X = {1, 3, 5} (even layers), Y = {2, 4, 6} (odd layers). Check: its cycles 1-2-3-4 and 1-4-5-6 both have even length.

visual.caption: Write each node's BFS layer next to it.

practice.hint: Run BFS from 1 and write each node's layer beside it. Then go through the 7 edges looking for one whose two ends share a layer.

practice.problem: BFS or DFS? (a) r has children x and y; y has child z; dashed r-z. (b) Path r, x, y, z; dashed x-z. (c) r has children x and y; x has child z; y has child w; dashed z-w. (d) Can a dashed edge ever pass both tests?
practice.answer: (a) DFS only: depths 0 and 2 skip a level, and r is z's ancestor. (b) DFS only: depths 1 and 3, and x is z's ancestor. (c) BFS only: z and w are both at depth 2 and neither is an ancestor of the other; DFS(z) would have made w its child. (d) No. Passing both means an ancestor exactly one level up, which is the parent, and that edge is already a tree edge.
practice.hint: For each dashed edge, ask two questions. Do the two depths differ by more than 1? Is one end an ancestor of the other?

practice.problem: (a) DAG with edges s -> x, s -> y, s -> z, x -> t, y -> t, z -> t. How many topological orderings? Must x come before y? (b) DAG with edges a -> b, a -> c, b -> d, c -> d. List every topological ordering.
practice.answer: (a) s first, t last, and x, y, z in any order: 3! = 6. No: there is no path between x and y, so either can come first. (b) Two: a, b, c, d and a, c, b, d. a must be first and d last; b and c are unordered.
practice.hint: Find what is forced first: who must be first, who must be last. Then ask which of the remaining nodes have no path between them; only those create choices.

practice.problem: Design an O(m + n) algorithm that outputs the fewest edges you must delete from an undirected graph G (n nodes, m edges) so that it has no cycles. Prove your number is right, then use it on the pictured graph.

visual.caption: n = 7, m = 7. Node 7 has no edges.

practice.hint: An acyclic graph with k components has exactly n - k edges. So first find k.
practice.answer: Count the components k with repeated BFS (O(m + n)), then output m - (n - k). Why it's enough: while a cycle remains, deleting any one of its edges keeps everything connected (the rest of the cycle still joins its ends), so you can delete down to a spanning forest with n - k edges. Why fewer won't do: an acyclic graph with k components has exactly n - k edges, so keeping more than n - k edges forces a cycle. For a connected graph this is m - (n - 1). On the pictured graph: n = 7, m = 7, and BFS finds k = 2 components ({1, ..., 6} and {7}), so delete 7 - (7 - 2) = 2 edges, one from each triangle (for example 3-1 and 6-4).

intro.big_idea: A greedy algorithm builds its answer one piece at a time, always grabbing whatever looks best right now and never taking it back. The real work is proving that short-sighted choice still ends up optimal.
intro.picture_this: Booking one meeting room: always say yes to the meeting that ends soonest, and the room frees up for as many other meetings as possible.
you_know_it_when: There's a natural 'best next pick' (earliest finish, cheapest edge, closest node)
Once you pick something you never need to undo it
Scheduling, shortest paths, spanning trees, making change

visual.caption: Sorted by finish time. Take each meeting that starts after the last one you took ends.

problems.title: Interval scheduling by earliest finish
problems.problem: Choose as many non-overlapping intervals as possible: A[1,4], B[3,5], C[0,6], D[5,7], E[3,9], F[5,9], G[6,10], H[8,11]. (Touching is fine: [1,4] and [4,6] don't overlap.)

visual.caption: Rows are already in finish-time order.

warmup.question: Three meetings: X [0, 5], Y [1, 2], Z [3, 4]. Which one ends first? How many can you fit in one room?
warmup.answer: Y ends first, at 2. Take Y, then Z (it starts at 3, after 2): 2 meetings. X overlaps both, so it can't join them.

walk.say: Sort by finish time: A (4), B (5), C (6), D (7), E (9), F (9), G (10), H (11). Keep one variable, end = the finish of the last interval taken. Start with end = 0.
walk.look: Notice: the rows run top to bottom in finish order, so we just sweep down once.

walk.say: A starts at 1, which is at or after end = 0. Take it, and set end = 4.
B starts at 3 and C starts at 0. Both start before end = 4, so they overlap A. Skip both.
D starts at 5, at or after 4. Take it, and set end = 7.
E (starts 3), F (starts 5) and G (starts 6) all start before end = 7. Skip them.
H starts at 8, at or after 7. Take it; end = 11. Answer: {A, D, H}, 3 intervals.
walk.look: Notice: one comparison per interval. After sorting, the sweep is O(n).

problems.why: Picking the interval that ends first leaves the most room for the rest. The 'greedy stays ahead' proof shows that after k picks, greedy's k-th interval ends no later than the k-th interval of any optimal solution, so greedy can always fit at least as many. Earliest start fails here: C starts first but blocks A, B and D.
problems.tip: Sort first. Lots of greedy algorithms are 'sort by the right thing, then sweep once'.

problems.title: Break a greedy rule with one counterexample
problems.problem: Interval scheduling: pick the most non-overlapping shows. Break two wrong rules. (1) Earliest start, on [0, 9], [1, 3], [4, 6], [7, 8]. (2) Shortest length, on [0, 4], [3, 5], [4, 8].

warmup.question: A rule says 'take the longest show first'. On [0, 10], [1, 2], [3, 4], what does it pick, and is that the best you can do?
warmup.answer: It takes [0, 10], and then nothing else fits: 1 show. But [1, 2] and [3, 4] together give 2, so the rule fails on this input.

walk.say: (1) Earliest start takes [0, 9] first, because it starts at 0. The rule only looks at start times, not at how long a show runs.
Every other show overlaps [0, 9], so the rule has to skip them all. It ends with 1 show.

visual.caption: earliest start: 1 show

walk.say: But [1, 3], [4, 6] and [7, 8] don't overlap each other: 3 shows. One input where the rule loses is a complete disproof.

visual.caption: better: 3 shows

walk.look: Notice the shape: one long show sitting on top of many short ones.

walk.say: (2) Shortest length takes [3, 5] (length 2; the other two have length 4). [0, 4] and [4, 8] both overlap it, so the rule ends with 1 show.

visual.caption: shortest length: 1 show

walk.say: But [0, 4] and [4, 8] are compatible: one ends exactly as the other starts. That's 2 shows. Answer: both rules fail, earliest start (1 vs 3) and shortest length (1 vs 2).

visual.caption: better: 2 shows

walk.look: Notice the shape: one short show straddling two long ones.

problems.why: One instance plus a better answer is a complete disproof. Shapes to remember: one long show covering many short ones breaks earliest start, and one short show straddling two long ones breaks shortest length. Earliest FINISH has no counterexample, and that needs a proof.
problems.tip: To break a greedy rule, build the smallest instance where its first pick blocks two good picks. Then run the rule to show it.

problems.title: Minimize the maximum lateness
problems.problem: Jobs: J1 (length 2, deadline 4), J2 (length 3, deadline 5), J3 (length 1, deadline 2), J4 (length 2, deadline 9). Find the maximum lateness L under earliest deadline first (EDF) and under shortest length first. Then prove EDF's answer is optimal without trying other orders.

visual.caption: One machine, start at time 0, one job at a time.

warmup.question: One job: length 3, deadline 2, starting at time 0. When does it finish, and how late is it?
warmup.answer: It finishes at 3, so it is 3 - 2 = 1 late. Lateness is finish minus deadline, or 0 if the job is on time.

walk.say: EDF sorts by deadline only, ignoring lengths: J3 (2), J1 (4), J2 (5), J4 (9).
walk.look: Notice: the deadline column now reads 2, 4, 5, 9 from top to bottom.

walk.say: Run them back to back from time 0, with no idle time. Each finish is the last finish plus this job's length: 1, 3, 6, 8.
Lateness = max(0, finish - deadline). J3, J1 and J4 are on time. J2 finishes at 6 with deadline 5: 1 late. So EDF has L = 1.

visual.caption: EDF: L = 1

walk.say: Shortest first: J3, J1, J4, J2. Finishes 1, 3, 5, 8. Now J2 finishes at 8 with deadline 5: 3 late. L = 3, worse.

visual.caption: shortest first: L = 3

walk.say: Can any order beat 1? J3, J1 and J2 need 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 time units, and the latest of their deadlines is 5. Whichever of them runs last finishes at 6 or later, so every order has L >= 1. Answer: EDF gives L = 1 and is optimal; shortest first gives L = 3.
walk.look: Notice: 6 units of work can't all fit before time 5.

problems.why: L is the worst single job, not a total. Idle time never helps, so a schedule is just an order. A quick lower bound (total work vs latest deadline of some group of jobs) lets you certify optimality without checking all n! orders.
problems.tip: Make a 4-column table: order, finish times, lateness of each, max. It's fast and it is exactly what graders check.

problems.title: Dijkstra by hand
problems.problem: Find the shortest distance from s to every node, and the shortest path to t. Edges: s->a 4, s->b 1, b->a 2, a->t 1, b->t 5.

visual.caption: All edge lengths are non-negative, so Dijkstra applies.

warmup.question: a's estimate is 4. You settle b at distance 1, and there is an edge b->a of length 2. What is a's new estimate?
warmup.answer: min(4, 1 + 2) = 3. 'Relaxing' an edge just means: keep the smaller of the old estimate and the new route through the node you settled.

walk.say: Start: d(s) = 0 and every other estimate is infinity. Pencil the estimates next to the nodes.
walk.look: Notice: yellow tags are estimates that can still fall; coral marks one that just changed. Teal means settled for good.

walk.say: Settle s, the smallest at 0. Check each edge out of s: a = 0 + 4 = 4, b = 0 + 1 = 1.
Settle b, the smallest unsettled estimate at 1. Relax b's edges: a = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3, and t = 1 + 5 = 6.
walk.look: Notice: a fell from 4 to 3. The route through b beats the direct edge.

walk.say: Settle a at 3 (smaller than t's 6). Relax a->t: t = min(6, 3 + 1) = 4.
Settle t at 4. Everything is settled. Answer: d(s) = 0, d(b) = 1, d(a) = 3, d(t) = 4. Follow prev back from t: t from a, a from b, b from s. Path s -> b -> a -> t, length 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.
walk.look: Notice: the shortest path uses 3 edges, while the 'direct-looking' routes cost 5 and 6.

problems.why: When Dijkstra settles the closest unsettled node, no other route can beat it: any other path has to leave the settled set through some edge, and with non-negative weights that already costs at least as much. Negative edges break this argument, which is why Bellman-Ford exists.
problems.tip: Pencil the tentative distances right onto the nodes, and lock in (settle) only the smallest one each round.

problems.title: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree
problems.problem: Find an MST. Edges: AB 1, BC 4, AC 3, CD 2, BD 5.

visual.caption: 4 nodes, so a spanning tree needs 3 edges.

warmup.question: Kruskal is about to look at edge B-C. The tree so far already has A-B and A-C. Add B-C or skip it?
warmup.answer: Skip it. B and C are already connected through A, so B-C would close the cycle A, B, C.

walk.say: Sort the edges from cheapest up: AB 1, CD 2, AC 3, BC 4, BD 5. At the start every node is its own piece (one color each).

visual.caption: next: AB 1

walk.look: Notice: the node colors show which piece each node is in.

walk.say: AB (1): A and B are in different pieces, so it can't make a cycle. Add it. A and B merge into one piece.

visual.caption: next: CD 2

walk.say: CD (2): C and D are in different pieces. Add it. Now there are two pieces, {A, B} and {C, D}.

visual.caption: next: AC 3

walk.say: AC (3): A is blue, C is pink, different pieces. Add it. Everything is one piece now, with 3 = n - 1 edges.

visual.caption: next: BC 4

walk.say: BC (4) and BD (5) each join two nodes that are already in the same piece, so each would close a cycle. Skip both. Answer: MST = {AB, CD, AC}, weight 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

visual.caption: MST weight 6

walk.look: Notice: once you have n - 1 edges you can stop reading the list.

problems.why: Cut property: for any split of the nodes into two groups, the cheapest edge crossing between them is in every MST (with distinct weights). Each time Kruskal adds an edge, it is the cheapest edge leaving one of its current components, so every edge it adds is safe.
problems.tip: Before adding an edge, ask one question: are its two ends already connected? If yes, skip it.

problems.title: Prim's algorithm by hand
problems.problem: Edges: A-C 1, B-C 2, D-E 3, A-B 4, B-D 5, C-D 8, C-E 9. Run Prim from D, listing the edges that cross the cut (tree, rest) at each step. Compare with Kruskal.

visual.caption: Start from D (yellow). 5 nodes, so the tree needs 4 edges.

warmup.question: The tree so far is just {A}. Edges: A-B 5, A-C 2, B-C 1. Which edge does Prim add first?
warmup.answer: A-C (2). Prim only looks at edges with exactly one end in the tree. B-C (1) is cheaper, but neither of its ends is in the tree yet.

walk.say: Tree {D}. The edges crossing from the tree to the rest are B-D 5, C-D 8 and D-E 3. The cheapest is D-E (3): add it.

visual.caption: tree {D}: pick D-E 3

walk.look: Notice: the yellow nodes are the tree. Only edges with exactly one yellow end are options.

walk.say: Tree {D, E}. Crossing edges: B-D 5, C-D 8, C-E 9. E brought in C-E. The cheapest is B-D (5): add it.

visual.caption: tree {D, E}: pick B-D 5

walk.say: Tree {B, D, E}. B brought in new options: A-B 4 and B-C 2, plus the old C-D 8 and C-E 9. The cheapest is B-C (2): add it.

visual.caption: tree {B, D, E}: pick B-C 2

walk.look: Notice: the list of crossing edges changes every round. Rewrite it each time.

walk.say: Tree {B, C, D, E}. Only A is left: A-B 4 and A-C 1 cross. (C-D and C-E are inside the tree now.) Add A-C (1).

visual.caption: tree {B, C, D, E}: pick A-C 1

walk.say: All 5 nodes are in, using 4 = n - 1 edges. Answer: MST {D-E, B-D, B-C, A-C}, cost 3 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 11. Kruskal check: A-C add, B-C add, D-E add, A-B skip (A and B already joined through C), B-D add. Same four edges, cost 11.

visual.caption: MST cost 11 (same set as Kruskal)

problems.why: Each Prim edge is, by construction, the cheapest edge crossing the cut (tree, everything else), so the cut property says it belongs to every MST. With distinct costs the MST is unique, so Prim and Kruskal must agree on the set (usually not on the order). Prim is Dijkstra with a different key: the single edge cost, not a path length. With a heap it runs in O(m log n).
problems.tip: Rewrite the full list of crossing edges at every step. The most common mistake is forgetting the new options the latest node brought in.

problems.title: Union-find inside Kruskal
problems.problem: Run Kruskal on A-C 1, B-C 2, D-E 3, A-B 4, B-D 5 using union-find. The smaller set's representative points at the larger set's; on a tie, the first set's representative points at the second's. Show each find, each decision and each pointer change, then give the final depth and check it against the log2 bound.

visual.caption: Start: every node is its own set and points to itself.

warmup.question: Pointers: A -> C and B -> C, and C points to itself. What is find(A)? Are A and B in the same set?
warmup.answer: find(A) follows A -> C and stops at C, which points to itself. find(B) is also C, so yes, they're in the same set, and an edge A-B would make a cycle.

walk.say: Edge A-C (1): find(A) = A and find(C) = C, different, so add the edge. Sizes are 1 and 1, a tie, so the first set's representative points at the second's: A -> C.

visual.caption: sets {A, C}, {B}, {D}, {E}

walk.look: Notice: teal nodes are representatives (they point to themselves). The tag is their set's size.

walk.say: Edge B-C (2): find(B) = B, find(C) = C: add. Size 1 vs 2, so the smaller set's rep points at the larger's: B -> C.

visual.caption: sets {A, B, C}, {D}, {E}

walk.say: Edge D-E (3): find(D) = D, find(E) = E: add. A tie at size 1, so D -> E.

visual.caption: sets {A, B, C}, {D, E}

walk.say: Edge A-B (4): find(A) follows A -> C, so it's C. find(B) follows B -> C, also C. Same representative means same set: skip, because the edge would close a cycle.

visual.caption: find(A) = find(B) = C: skip A-B

walk.look: Notice: both yellow find paths end at C. The cycle check is just 'do the two finds match?'

walk.say: Edge B-D (5): find(B) = C, find(D) = E (D -> E). Different: add. Sizes 3 vs 2, so E (the smaller set's rep) points at C. One set now: done.

visual.caption: one set: {A, B, C, D, E}

walk.say: Answer: Kruskal added A-C, B-C, D-E, B-D and skipped A-B. The deepest node is D: D -> E -> C, depth 2. log2(5) is about 2.32, so depth 2 is within the bound.

visual.caption: deepest: D, 2 pointers from C

walk.look: Notice: D's depth rose only when its set {D, E} was the smaller one in a merge.

problems.why: Union by size keeps depth <= log2 k for a set of k nodes: a node's depth rises only when its set is the smaller one in a merge, so its set at least doubles every time. That makes find O(log n), and Kruskal is O(m log n) overall (sorting plus m finds). Without the rule, merging into a growing chain can make depth n - 1.
problems.tip: Write the sets after every edge. The cycle check is just 'do the two finds match?'

problems.title: Greedy stays ahead, on real numbers
problems.problem: Earliest-finish greedy picked A [1, 3], C [4, 6], D [6, 7], F [7, 9]. Another solution with 4 shows is O = A [1, 3], C [4, 6], D [6, 7], G [8, 10]. Write the stays-ahead claim, prove the base case, and carry out the inductive step for r = 4 using these numbers. Then explain why greedy can't have fewer shows than an optimum.

visual.caption: Teal: greedy's picks i_r. Lavender: O's picks j_r.
