warmup.question: Greedy's 2nd show ends at 6. Some other solution's 3rd show starts at 7. Is that show available for greedy's 3rd pick?
warmup.answer: Yes. It starts at 7, after greedy's last show ends at 6, so it overlaps nothing greedy has chosen. Greedy's 3rd pick then ends no later than it does.

walk.say: Line the two solutions up by position. The claim to prove: f(i_r) <= f(j_r) for every r. Greedy's r-th show finishes no later than O's r-th show.
walk.look: Notice: the claim compares the two finish columns, row by row.

walk.say: Base case, r = 1: greedy's first pick has the earliest finish of ALL shows, so f(i_1) = 3 <= f(j_1) = 3.
Inductive step for r = 4. The hypothesis is the claim for r - 1 = 3: f(i_3) = 7 <= f(j_3) = 7. (Rows 2 and 3 work the same way.)

O is compatible, so G starts after D ends: s(j_4) = 8 >= f(j_3) = 7. Chain it with the hypothesis: s(j_4) = 8 >= 7 = f(i_3). So G overlaps nothing greedy had chosen. It was available for greedy's 4th pick.

visual.caption: G starts at 8, after greedy's D ends at 7

walk.look: Notice: G's bar starts to the right of the dashed line, so it was free to choose.

walk.say: Greedy took the available show with the earliest finish, F. G was one of the options, so f(i_4) = 9 <= f(j_4) = 10.

Finish: suppose O had a 5th show. It would start at or after f(j_4) = 10 >= f(i_4) = 9, so it would still be available to greedy. Greedy only stops when nothing is available, so it can't have fewer shows than O. Answer: greedy is optimal (k = m = 4).

visual.caption: any j_5 would also fit after greedy's F

walk.look: Notice: being ahead means greedy can't run out of room before O does.

problems.why: The pattern: define a measure of progress (finish time of the r-th pick), prove by induction that greedy is at least as far along at every step, then argue that being ahead means greedy can't run out early. The general proof is these lines with letters instead of numbers.
problems.tip: If you freeze on the proof, make this table for a small example and read off what each line has to say.

problems.title: The exchange argument for EDF
problems.problem: Prove that earliest deadline first minimizes the maximum lateness. Then watch the proof's process on jobs J1 (2, d 4), J2 (3, d 5), J3 (1, d 2), J4 (2, d 9), starting from the bad order J4, J2, J1, J3.

visual.caption: Deadlines: J3 2, J1 4, J2 5, J4 9. This order runs them latest-deadline first.

warmup.question: J2 (deadline 5) runs right before J1 (deadline 4). Is that pair an inversion? What about J1 right before J2?
warmup.answer: J2 before J1 is an inversion: the later deadline runs first. J1 before J2 is fine. An EDF order is exactly an order with no inversions.

walk.say: An inversion is a pair where i runs before j but d(j) < d(i). In J4, J2, J1, J3 the deadlines read 9, 5, 4, 2, all backwards: all 6 pairs are inverted. If an order has any inversion, it has one between neighbors.

visual.caption: 6 inversions

walk.say: Swap one neighboring inversion, J4 and J2. Only those two move: everything before and after them finishes at exactly the same time. The swap removes exactly one inversion.
walk.look: Notice: the dashed line. The swapped pair ends at the same moment, so J1 and J3 don't move.

walk.say: Why the swap is no worse, in general (i before j, d(j) < d(i)): j now finishes earlier, so its lateness can only drop. i now finishes at f(j), j's old finish, so its lateness is f(j) - d(i) <= f(j) - d(j), which is j's OLD lateness.

lines.label: f(j): old end of j = new end of i

walk.say: Keep swapping neighboring inversions. Each swap removes one, and L never goes up: 6, 6, 6, 4, 4, 1, 1. After 6 swaps there are no inversions left: J3, J1, J2, J4, which is EDF.
Notice the first two swaps gain nothing (L stays 6). A swap is only 'no worse', never promised to be better. That's why the 'swap to get something strictly better, contradiction' proof is wrong.

visual.caption: L at each step (0 = the start)

walk.say: Answer (the proof): start from ANY optimal order O. Swap neighboring inversions one at a time; each swap keeps L the same or lower, so O stays optimal. After at most n(n - 1)/2 swaps there are no inversions: an EDF order. All EDF orders have the same L, so EDF is optimal.

visual.caption: 0 inversions, L = 1

walk.look: Notice: deadlines now read 2, 4, 5, 9, left to right.

problems.why: The tempting proof ('swap an inversion in the optimum to get something better, contradiction') fails, because the swap may leave L unchanged. The correct argument turns the optimum into EDF one swap at a time without ever getting worse, and the inversion count guarantees the process ends.
problems.tip: Write 'no worse AND one step closer to greedy'. Both halves are needed; graders take points if you claim 'strictly better'.

problems.title: The cut property: repair a spanning tree
problems.problem: Same graph: A-C 1, B-C 2, D-E 3, A-B 4, B-D 5, C-D 8, C-E 9. Take the cut S = {A, B}. Its cheapest crossing edge is e = A-C. Start from the spanning tree T = {A-B, B-C, B-D, D-E}, which leaves e out. Repair T the way the cut property proof does, then show what goes wrong with the wrong swap.

visual.caption: T in bold (cost 14). e = A-C, dashed, is not in T.

warmup.question: Cut S = {A, B}. Edges: A-C 1, B-C 2, B-D 5, A-B 4. Which edges cross the cut, and which crossing edge is cheapest?
warmup.answer: A-C, B-C and B-D cross: one end in S, one end outside. A-B stays inside S. The cheapest crossing edge is A-C (1).

walk.say: The setup. cost(T) = 4 + 2 + 5 + 3 = 14. The edges crossing the cut S = {A, B} are A-C 1, B-C 2 and B-D 5. The cheapest is e = A-C, and T leaves it out.

visual.caption: crossing edges in coral (T's) and dashed (e)

walk.look: Notice: T uses two crossing edges, B-C and B-D. Only one of them is the right one to remove.

walk.say: Find T's path between e's endpoints, A and C. In T it is A, B, C (A-B, then B-C). T is a tree, so this path is the only one.

visual.caption: T's path from A to C: A, B, C

walk.say: Walk that path and find the first edge that crosses the cut. A-B stays inside S. B-C crosses. So e' = B-C.

visual.caption: e' = B-C: on the path AND crossing

walk.look: Notice: the path starts inside S and ends outside, so it has to cross somewhere.

walk.say: Swap: T' = T + A-C - B-C = {A-B, A-C, B-D, D-E}. Adding A-C makes the one cycle A, B, C, A; removing B-C breaks it. cost(T') = 14 - 2 + 1 = 13 < 14, so T was not a minimum spanning tree.

visual.caption: T' costs 13: still a spanning tree, and cheaper

walk.say: The wrong swap: B-D also crosses the cut, but it is NOT on T's path from A to C. T + A-C - B-D = {A-B, B-C, A-C, D-E} keeps the cycle A, B, C and cuts D and E off. Not a tree at all.

visual.caption: cycle A, B, C, and {D, E} cut off

walk.say: Answer: the repair is T' = {A-B, A-C, B-D, D-E}, cost 13. Remove the crossing edge on T's path between e's endpoints (B-C); removing B-D, which is off the path, breaks the tree. The same swap improves any spanning tree that leaves out A-C, so A-C is in every MST.

problems.why: Cut property: the cheapest edge crossing any cut is in every MST. The proof adds e to T, which creates exactly one cycle, and removes the crossing edge e' ON T's path between e's endpoints. Only that choice is guaranteed to break the cycle and keep things connected.
problems.tip: Say the exact phrase 'the crossing edge on T's path between e's endpoints'. Graders look for it.

practice.problem: Choose as many non-overlapping intervals as possible: A[0,3], B[2,4], C[3,6], D[1,7], E[6,8], F[5,9], G[8,10].
practice.answer: By finish time: A(3), B(4), C(6), D(7), E(8), F(9), G(10). Take A, skip B, take C (3 >= 3), skip D, take E (6 >= 6), skip F, take G (8 >= 8). Answer: {A, C, E, G}, 4 intervals.
practice.hint: Sort by finish time and keep one variable, end. Take an interval only if it starts at or after end; touching counts as fine.

practice.problem: Break each greedy rule with one small counterexample. (a) Coins worth 1, 3 and 4: 'always take the largest coin that fits' to make change with the fewest coins. (b) Earliest deadline first, used to minimize TOTAL lateness (the sum, not the max). Use three jobs.
practice.answer: (a) Amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), but 3 + 3 uses 2. (b) X (length 10, deadline 1), Y (length 1, deadline 2), Z (length 1, deadline 3). EDF runs X, Y, Z: finishes 10, 11, 12, lateness 9, 9, 9, total 27. Running Y, Z, X: finishes 1, 2, 12, lateness 0, 0, 11, total 11.

panels.caption: (a) coins 1, 3, 4: pick an amount, then fill in greedy's coins and a better set
(b) three jobs: make up lengths and deadlines that trap EDF

practice.hint: (a) Look for a small amount where grabbing a 4 forces 1s, but 3s fit exactly. (b) Give the job with the earliest deadline a huge length.

practice.problem: Jobs (length, deadline): 1 (3, 4), 2 (2, 6), 3 (1, 3), 4 (4, 9), 5 (2, 8). Find the max lateness under (a) earliest deadline first, (b) shortest length first (ties by job number), (c) smallest slack d - t first. (d) Argue, without trying other orders, that the EDF answer is optimal.
practice.answer: (a) EDF order 3, 1, 2, 5, 4: finishes 1, 4, 6, 8, 12; lateness 0, 0, 0, 0, 3; L = 3. (b) Shortest first 3, 2, 5, 1, 4: finishes 1, 3, 5, 8, 12; job 1 finishes at 8 with deadline 4, so it is 4 late; L = 4. (c) Slack d - t: job 1: 1, job 3: 2, job 2: 4, job 4: 5, job 5: 6, so order 1, 3, 2, 4, 5: finishes 3, 4, 6, 10, 12; lateness 0, 1, 0, 1, 4 (job 5 finishes at 12 with deadline 8); L = 4. (d) The jobs total 12 time units and every deadline is at most 9, so whichever job runs last finishes at 12 and is at least 3 late in every order. EDF gets 3, so it is optimal.

visual.caption: Fill the EDF rows first; then do (b) and (c) the same way.

practice.hint: For EDF, sort by deadline only and add lengths as you go. For (d), compare the total of all the lengths with the largest deadline.

practice.problem: Run Dijkstra from s. Edges: s->a 2, s->b 6, a->b 3, a->c 7, b->c 1, c->t 2, b->t 6.
practice.answer: Settle s (0): a = 2, b = 6. Settle a (2): b = min(6, 2 + 3) = 5, c = 2 + 7 = 9. Settle b (5): c = min(9, 5 + 1) = 6, t = 5 + 6 = 11. Settle c (6): t = min(11, 6 + 2) = 8. Settle t (8). Distances: a 2, b 5, c 6, t 8. Path to t: s -> a -> b -> c -> t (2 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 8).

visual.caption: Write each tentative distance next to its node; update in pencil.

practice.hint: Settle s first, then always the unsettled node with the smallest estimate. Expect b's estimate to drop once a is settled.

practice.problem: Find an MST with Kruskal. Edges: AB 2, AC 3, BC 1, BD 4, CD 5, DE 6, CE 7.
practice.answer: In sorted order: BC 1 (add), AB 2 (add), AC 3 (cycle, skip), BD 4 (add), CD 5 (cycle, skip), DE 6 (add), CE 7 (skip). MST = {BC, AB, BD, DE}, weight 13.
practice.hint: Sort the 7 edges by weight. Before each one ask: are its ends already connected? You can stop once you have n - 1 = 4 edges.

practice.problem: Graph W, distinct weights: P-R 1, Q-S 2, Q-R 3, P-Q 4, R-T 5, R-S 6, S-T 7, S-U 8, T-U 9. (a) Run Prim from P, listing the crossing edges at each step. (b) For the cut ({P, Q}, everything else), give the cutset and the edge the cut property forces into the MST.
practice.answer: (a) {P}: P-R 1, P-Q 4, pick P-R. {P, R}: P-Q 4, Q-R 3, R-S 6, R-T 5, pick Q-R. {P, Q, R}: Q-S 2, R-S 6, R-T 5, pick Q-S. {P, Q, R, S}: R-T 5, S-T 7, S-U 8, pick R-T. {P, Q, R, S, T}: S-U 8, T-U 9, pick S-U. MST {P-R, Q-R, Q-S, R-T, S-U}, weight 1 + 3 + 2 + 5 + 8 = 19 (Kruskal gives the same set). (b) Cutset P-R 1, Q-S 2, Q-R 3 (P-Q lies inside the cut). The cut property forces P-R.

visual.caption: Graph W. Prim starts at P.

practice.hint: Shade the tree as it grows. Each round, list every edge with exactly one shaded end, then take the cheapest.

practice.problem: Start with singletons 1 to 8. Do Union(1,2), Union(3,4), Union(1,3), Union(5,6), Union(7,8), Union(5,7), Union(1,5), renaming the smaller set and breaking ties by pointing the first set's representative at the second's. What is the final depth, and how does it compare with log2(8)? What goes wrong if the LARGER set is renamed instead?
practice.answer: Pointers: 1 -> 2, 3 -> 4, 2 -> 4 (tie at size 2), 5 -> 6, 7 -> 8, 6 -> 8 (tie at size 2), 4 -> 8 (tie at size 4). The path 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8 gives depth 3 = log2(8): the bound is tight because every union merged equal sizes. If the LARGER set is renamed instead, repeatedly merging a singleton into a growing set builds a chain of depth n - 1, so find becomes O(n) instead of O(log n).

visual.caption: Start: 8 singletons. Draw each pointer as you go.

practice.hint: Write each set's size next to its representative. For Union(1, 3), first find both representatives: 2 and 4, both of size 2, so it's a tie.

practice.problem: Shows: 1 [0, 6], 2 [1, 3], 3 [2, 5], 4 [4, 7], 5 [5, 9], 6 [6, 8], 7 [8, 11], 8 [9, 10]. (a) Run earliest finish with the variable end. (b) Another optimal solution is O = {2, 6, 7}. Line greedy and O up by position and carry out the inductive step for r = 2 with real numbers.
practice.answer: (a) Sorted by finish: 2 (3), 3 (5), 1 (6), 4 (7), 6 (8), 5 (9), 8 (10), 7 (11). Take 2 (end 3); skip 3 and 1; take 4 (end 7); skip 6 and 5; take 8 (end 10); skip 7. Greedy = {2, 4, 8}, 3 shows. (b) Finishes: greedy 3, 7, 10; O 3, 8, 11. Step r = 2: hypothesis f(i_1) = 3 <= f(j_1) = 3. O is compatible, so s(j_2) = 6 >= f(j_1) = 3 >= f(i_1) = 3, so show 6 was available at greedy's 2nd pick. Greedy took the earliest-finishing available show, so f(i_2) = 7 <= f(j_2) = 8.

visual.caption: Mark greedy's picks, then O = {2, 6, 7}.

practice.hint: Sort by finish first. For (b), write both solutions' finish times side by side, then chain s(j_2) >= f(j_1) >= f(i_1).

practice.problem: Jobs have lengths t(j) and no deadlines. The goal is to minimize the SUM of finish times. Prove with an exchange argument that shortest job first is optimal.
practice.answer: Let A be shortest-first, and take any optimal O different from A. Then O has adjacent jobs i then j with t(i) > t(j). Swap them to get O'. Every other job finishes at the same time. If the pair starts at S, before the swap it contributes (S + t(i)) + (S + t(i) + t(j)); after, (S + t(j)) + (S + t(j) + t(i)). The difference is t(i) - t(j) > 0, so O' is strictly better, contradicting O optimal. So an optimal order has no such pair, which means it is shortest-first (equal lengths can go in either order without changing the sum), and A is optimal.

visual.caption: Example with t(i) = 4 > t(j) = 1, starting at S = 2. Write each finish time under its block.

practice.hint: Swap one neighboring pair i, j with t(i) > t(j). Only those two finish times change; write both sums starting from the same time S.

practice.problem: True or false, with reasons (positive weights). (a) The heaviest edge in a graph is never in an MST. (b) With distinct weights, the lightest edge is in every MST. (c) Treat a graph as undirected. The tree of Dijkstra's prev edges from s is always an MST.
practice.answer: (a) False: if the heaviest edge is the only edge reaching some node (like z-w, weight 10), every spanning tree must contain it. (b) True: take the cut S = {u} for one endpoint u. The lightest edge overall is the lightest edge crossing that cut, so the cut property puts it in every MST. (c) False: in the triangle s-a 2, s-b 2, a-b 1, Dijkstra's tree from s uses s-a and s-b (cost 4), but the MST is a-b plus one s edge (cost 3).
practice.hint: (a) Look at node w in the first picture. (b) Choose the cut that puts one endpoint of the lightest edge alone. (c) Run Dijkstra from s, then Kruskal.

intro.big_idea: Split the problem into smaller copies of itself, solve those (by splitting again), then glue the answers together. The running time is the work on every level of the split, added up.
intro.picture_this: Sorting a tall pile of exams with friends: split the pile in half, hand off each half, then merge the two sorted stacks back into one.
you_know_it_when: The problem on half the input looks just like the original
Combining two half-answers is easier than starting from scratch
A recurrence like T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

visual.caption: Sorting 8 items: each level touches all 8 once, and halving 8 down to 1 takes 3 splits.

problems.title: Mergesort: the same work on every level
problems.problem: Trace mergesort on [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 8, 6] and count how many elements each level of merging places. Then solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, T(1) = 1.

visual.caption: 8 numbers to sort. Mergesort halves the list until every piece has one number, then merges back up.

warmup.question: Merge the sorted lists [2, 5] and [4, 7] into one sorted list. How many elements do you place into the output?
warmup.answer: [2, 4, 5, 7]. You place 4 elements, one per step, so merging costs about the total length of the two lists.

walk.say: Split the list in half, then split each half again, until every piece is a single number. A single number is already sorted, so this is where the recursion stops.
walk.look: Notice: 8 to 4 to 2 to 1 is three halvings, because log2 8 = 3.

walk.say: Bottom merging level: merge each pair of singles. That is 4 merges of 2 elements, so 8 elements placed in total.
walk.look: Notice: every one of the 8 numbers was placed exactly once on this level.

walk.say: Next level: merge the pairs into sorted fours. 2 merges of 4 elements: again 8 elements placed.
Top level: one merge of the two fours places all 8 elements. Three merging levels, 8 each: 24 placements.
walk.look: Notice: each row costs 8, and there are log2 8 = 3 merging rows.

walk.say: Now any n. The root merges n elements. Level 1 has 2 problems of size n/2, doing 2 x n/2 = n. Level 2 has 4 x n/4 = n. Level k has 2^k problems of size n/2^k: still n.
walk.look: Notice: twice as many problems, each half as big, so every level adds up to n.

walk.say: The size halves each level, so it reaches 1 after log2 n levels. That gives log2 n merging levels at n each, plus n leaves at T(1) = 1 each.

visual.caption: log2 n merging levels, n work on each.

walk.say: Answer: T(n) = n log2 n + n = Theta(n log n). Check n = 8: 8 x 3 + 8 = 32, and the recurrence gives T(8) = 2T(4) + 8 = 2 x 12 + 8 = 32.

visual.caption: The formula matches the recurrence exactly.

walk.look: Notice: both rows agree for every n.

problems.why: Every level does the same total work n, because the pieces multiply exactly as fast as they shrink (2 pieces, each half the size). So the total is (work per level) x (number of levels) = n x log2 n. This balanced case is the one behind mergesort.
problems.tip: Write each level's total work on the side of the tree, then spot the pattern: same, shrinking, or growing.

problems.title: Count inversions with merge-and-count
problems.problem: Count the inversions in [3, 1, 4, 2] (pairs i < j with a_i > a_j) using merge-and-count.

visual.caption: Split in half. Each half has one inversion inside it; the merge finds the rest.

warmup.question: An inversion is a pair of positions i < j with a_i > a_j (a bigger number before a smaller one). List the inversions in [2, 3, 1].
warmup.answer: (2, 1) and (3, 1): the 1 comes after two bigger numbers. That's 2 inversions.

walk.say: Split [3, 1, 4, 2] into a left half [3, 1] and a right half [4, 2]. Every inversion is inside the left, inside the right, or crosses from left to right.
Recurse on each half. [3, 1] has 1 inversion and comes back sorted as [1, 3]. [4, 2] has 1 inversion and comes back as [2, 4]. Count so far: 2.
walk.look: Notice: the halves come back sorted, which is what makes the merge easy to count.

walk.say: Merge. Compare 1 and 2: take 1 from the left. Taking from the left never jumps over anything, so add 0.
Compare 3 and 2: take 2 from the right. It jumps over every left element still waiting (just the 3), so add 1. Count: 3.
walk.look: Notice: the 3 still waiting on the left is the element that 2 jumps.

walk.say: Take 3 (left), then 4 (right). When 4 is taken the left list is empty, so it jumps nothing. No more additions.
Total: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 inversions: (3, 1), (3, 2) and (4, 2). The merge also hands back the sorted list, so a parent call can keep counting the same way.

visual.caption: Each arc is one inversion: a bigger number before a smaller one.

walk.look: Notice: one pink arc inside each half, plus the coral crossing arc found by the merge.

problems.why: When you take an element from the right half, it is smaller than everything left in the left half, and all of those come before it in the original array. So you can count many inversions at once while merging, and the whole thing stays O(n log n).
problems.tip: Each time you take from the right half, count how many left-half elements are still waiting: that's how many inversions it just jumped.

problems.title: A recurrence where the root wins
problems.problem: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2, T(1) = 1, by unrolling the recursion tree.

visual.caption: Each level does half the work of the one above, so the total is under 2n^2.

warmup.question: Add up 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... forever. Does the sum ever pass 2?
warmup.answer: No. It creeps toward 2 but never reaches it. A shrinking geometric series is at most a constant times its first term.

walk.say: Level 0 is the root: one problem of size n, doing n^2 work.
Level 1: two problems of size n/2. Each does (n/2)^2 = n^2/4, so the level does 2 x n^2/4 = n^2/2. Half of the root.
Level 2: four problems of size n/4, each doing (n/4)^2 = n^2/16. The level does 4 x n^2/16 = n^2/4. Each level is half the one above.
walk.look: Notice: the level totals on the right halve as you go down.

walk.say: Level k: 2^k problems, each of size n/2^k doing (n/2^k)^2 = n^2/4^k. The level total is 2^k x n^2/4^k = n^2/2^k.
Add the levels: n^2 (1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ...) < 2n^2. The bars show it with the root's work as 16 units: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
walk.look: Notice: the root's bar is as long as all the others put together, plus one.

walk.say: So n^2 <= T(n) < 2n^2: T(n) = Theta(n^2). The top level dominates, and the total is just a constant times the root's work.

visual.caption: Everything together (31) stays under twice the root.

problems.why: Here the work per level SHRINKS geometrically going down, so the top level dominates and the total is a constant times the root's work. Compare: equal work per level (mergesort) gives work x levels = n log n; growing work per level means the leaves dominate.
problems.tip: Write the work on each level as a fraction of the root's work. A shrinking ratio means root wins; ratio 1 means multiply by log n; growing means count the leaves.

problems.title: A recurrence where the leaves win
problems.problem: Solve T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n.

visual.caption: The work grows by 3/2 per level, so the bottom level wins: about n^1.585 in total.

warmup.question: In T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n, the root does n work. Level 1 has 3 problems of size n/2. What is level 1's total work? More or less than the root?
warmup.answer: 3 x n/2 = 1.5n, more than n. Three pieces that are only half as small add up to more work than the one big piece.

walk.say: Level 0: one problem of size n, doing n work.
Level 1: three problems of size n/2, so 3 x n/2 = 1.5n. That is MORE than the root.
walk.look: Notice: the level total went up, not down.

walk.say: Level 2: nine problems of size n/4, so 9 x n/4 = 2.25n. Every level is 3/2 times the one above.

visual.caption: Only one node's children are drawn; every n/2 node has 3 of its own.

walk.say: Level k has 3^k problems of size n/2^k: n (3/2)^k work. For n = 16 the levels do 16, 24, 36, 54, then 81 leaves. A growing series is dominated by its LAST term.
walk.look: Notice: the bottom bar (the 81 leaves) is the longest.

walk.say: The bottom is at depth log2 n, and it has 3^(log2 n) leaves. Rewrite that: 3^(log2 n) = n^(log2 3), about n^1.585.

visual.caption: Each time n doubles, the leaves triple: n^(log2 3).

walk.look: Notice: doubling n multiplies the leaf count by 3, not by 2.

walk.say: Answer: T(n) = Theta(n^(log2 3)), about Theta(n^1.585). The leaves win because 3 subproblems beat the shrink factor 2.

visual.caption: n^1.585 grows faster than n log n but slower than n^2.

problems.why: Compare the branching factor (3) with how much the size shrinks (2). More subproblems than the shrink factor means the work grows going down the tree and the leaves dominate. This is the recurrence behind fast integer multiplication (3 half-size multiplications instead of 4).
problems.tip: Compare the number of subproblems (a) with the shrink factor (b): a = b balanced, a > b the leaves win, a < b the top wins.

problems.title: Karatsuba: three multiplications instead of four
problems.problem: Multiply x = 23 by y = 41 using only three single-digit products, the Karatsuba way. Then give the recurrence for n-digit numbers and solve it.

visual.caption: Find ad + bc without ever computing ad or bc.

warmup.question: Multiply out (a + b)(c + d).
warmup.answer: ac + ad + bc + bd. So if you already know ac and bd, subtracting them leaves exactly ad + bc.

walk.say: Split each number into tens and ones: x = 23 gives a = 2, b = 3, and y = 41 gives c = 4, d = 1.
School method: xy = ac x 100 + (ad + bc) x 10 + bd. That needs four products: ac = 8, ad = 2, bc = 12, bd = 3.

visual.caption: Four multiplications. Can we skip the two coral ones?

walk.look: Notice: we only need the SUM ad + bc, not ad and bc separately.

walk.say: Karatsuba's trick: compute ac = 8 and bd = 3, then just ONE more product, (a + b)(c + d) = 5 x 5 = 25.
Subtract: ad + bc = 25 - 8 - 3 = 14. Three multiplications instead of four.
walk.look: Notice: 14 = 2 + 12, the same as ad + bc from the school method.

walk.say: For n-digit numbers each half has n/2 digits. Three half-size products plus O(n) adding and shifting: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n).
That is the leaves-win case: 3^(log2 n) = n^(log2 3), about n^1.59. Four products would give 4^(log2 n) = n^2, no better than school.
walk.look: Notice: the gap between the curves keeps widening as n grows.

problems.why: The obvious split needs four half-size products: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n = Theta(n^2), no better than grade-school multiplication. Saving one product per level changes the number of leaves from 4^(log2 n) = n^2 to 3^(log2 n) = n^1.59, a real asymptotic win.
problems.tip: When a D&C recurrence is a T(n/b) + n with a > b, the answer is n^(log_b a). Count leaves: a^(log_b n).

problems.title: Find a peak in O(log n)
problems.problem: A peak in array A[0..n-1] is an entry at least as big as its neighbors (the ends have one neighbor). Give an O(log n) algorithm, prove it correct, and run it on A = [2, 4, 7, 9, 8, 5, 3, 6].

visual.caption: Peaks here: 9 (index 3) and 6 (index 7). We only need to find one.

warmup.question: A peak is an entry at least as big as each neighbor (an end has one neighbor). Which entries of [1, 3, 4, 2] are peaks?
warmup.answer: Only 4 (index 2): it beats 3 and 2. The end 1 loses to 3, and the end 2 loses to 4.

walk.say: Algorithm: keep a range [lo, hi], starting with the whole array. Look at mid = floor((lo + hi)/2). If A[mid] < A[mid + 1], uphill is to the right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise hi = mid.
lo = 0, hi = 7, mid = 3. A[3] = 9 is bigger than A[4] = 8, so going right is downhill. Keep the left part: hi = 3.
walk.look: Notice: the right half is faded; we never look at it again.

walk.say: lo = 0, hi = 3, mid = 1. A[1] = 4 < A[2] = 7, so uphill is to the right: lo = 2.
lo = 2, hi = 3, mid = 2. A[2] = 7 < A[3] = 9, uphill again: lo = 3. Now lo = hi = 3, so we stop.
Why it is right. Invariant: the entry just left of lo is smaller than A[lo] (or lo = 0), and the entry just right of hi is smaller than A[hi] (or hi = n - 1). Both moves keep it true.

visual.caption: After step 2: A[4] = 8 is smaller than A[hi] = 9, exactly as the invariant says.

walk.look: Notice: the coral cell just outside the range is always smaller than the end it touches.

walk.say: When lo = hi, the invariant says both neighbors are smaller: A[3] = 9 is a peak. The range halves each step, so T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n).
walk.look: Notice: 9 beats both 7 and 8.

problems.why: You never need to see the whole array, only which way is 'uphill' at mid. Walking uphill from mid must reach a peak before falling off the range, and the invariant is the exam-ready way to say that. Binary search works on any problem where one comparison tells you which half still contains an answer.
problems.tip: For any binary search proof, state the invariant about lo and hi in one line, then check: true at start, kept by both branches, gives the answer at the end.

problems.title: Prove a recurrence bound by induction
problems.problem: Suppose T(2) <= c and T(n) <= 2T(n/2) + cn for n > 2 (n a power of 2). Prove T(n) <= cn log2 n for all n >= 2 by induction (the 'guess and check' method).

visual.caption: The tree suggests the guess cn log2 n; induction makes it a proof.

warmup.question: Write log2(n/2) in terms of log2 n. Check it with n = 8.
warmup.answer: log2(n/2) = log2 n - 1. For n = 8: log2 4 = 2 = 3 - 1. Halving the input removes exactly one level.

walk.say: Guess first. The recursion tree has about cn work on each of log2 n levels, so guess T(n) <= cn log2 n.

visual.caption: Same work cn on every level: the guess is cn log2 n.

walk.say: Base case n = 2: T(2) <= c, and the guess allows c x 2 x log2 2 = 2c. Since c <= 2c, the claim holds.

visual.caption: With c = 1: T(2) <= 1 and T(n) <= 2T(n/2) + n.

walk.look: Notice: with c = 1 the bound 1 sits under the guess 2.

walk.say: Inductive hypothesis: assume T(m) <= cm log2 m for every power of 2 with 2 <= m < n. We only need it for m = n/2.
walk.look: Notice: the hypothesis is used on the two smaller calls only.

walk.say: Plug it in: T(n) <= 2T(n/2) + cn <= 2 x c(n/2) log2(n/2) + cn = cn log2(n/2) + cn.

visual.caption: With c = 1: T(2) <= 1 and T(n) <= 2T(n/2) + n.

walk.say: Use log2(n/2) = log2 n - 1: cn(log2 n - 1) + cn = cn log2 n - cn + cn = cn log2 n. The -cn and +cn cancel exactly.

visual.caption: With c = 1: T(2) <= 1 and T(n) <= 2T(n/2) + n.

walk.look: Notice: the top row never passes the teal guess row.

walk.say: So T(n) <= cn log2 n for every power of 2 with n >= 2: T(n) = O(n log n). Each case leans only on the smaller case before it, like dominoes.

problems.why: Unrolling the tree finds the answer; induction proves it. The step works because the guess is exactly strong enough: the -cn from log2(n/2) cancels the +cn of the merge. A common mistake is using the claim for n itself in the step instead of for n/2.
problems.tip: Write the hypothesis for n/2 explicitly, substitute it, and simplify until the right side matches your guess exactly.

problems.title: Closest pair of points
problems.problem: Points: left half (1, 1), (2, 6), (4, 3), (5, 7); right half (6, 6), (7, 2), (9, 5), (10, 1), split by the line x = 5.5. The closest pair within each half has squared distance 10. Finish the combine step: which points go in the strip, which pairs do you check, and what is the answer? Then give the running time.

visual.caption: Blue = left half, pink = right half. Dashed: the best pair inside each half (squared distance 10).

warmup.question: What is the squared distance between (5, 7) and (6, 6)? Is it smaller than 10?
warmup.answer: (6 - 5)^2 + (6 - 7)^2 = 1 + 1 = 2, much smaller than 10. Squared distances compare the same way as distances, with no square roots.

walk.say: Each half has already found its best pair: (2, 6)-(5, 7) on the left and (6, 6)-(9, 5) on the right, both squared distance 10. So delta = sqrt(10), about 3.16.
walk.look: Notice: neither dashed pair crosses the gray line x = 5.5.

walk.say: A pair closer than delta must cross the line, with both points within delta of it. Keep points with 2.34 < x < 8.66: (4, 3), (5, 7), (6, 6), (7, 2).
walk.look: Notice: the four faded points are too far from the line to help.

walk.say: Sort the strip points by y: (7, 2), (4, 3), (6, 6), (5, 7). Each point now only needs checking against the next few (at most 7) in this order.
Compare each point with the ones after it in y order. With only 4 points that is every pair: 10, 17, 29, 13, 17 and 2.

visual.caption: Squared distances between strip points, in y order.

walk.look: Notice: the teal 2 is the only value below delta squared = 10.

walk.say: Best: (5, 7) and (6, 6) at squared distance 2, distance sqrt(2), about 1.41. It crosses the line and beats delta, so it is the closest pair overall.
Time: sort by x and by y once up front, O(n log n). Then each call splits, recurses twice, and does an O(n) strip pass: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).

problems.why: The key fact is that each strip point only needs to be compared with a constant number of the points after it in y order. Split the strip into delta/2 x delta/2 boxes: each box holds at most one point (two points in one box would be closer than delta, inside one half). Any point more than a couple of box rows above is farther than delta. K&T uses 15 as the constant; tighter counting gives 7. Either way the combine step is O(n).
problems.tip: Squared distances keep the arithmetic in whole numbers. Only take square roots when you set the strip width.

practice.problem: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, T(1) = 1. Write each level's total work beside the tree, then add the levels.

visual.caption: Each node does 1 unit of work. Fill in each level's total, then add them up.

practice.hint: Each node does 1 unit of work no matter how big its problem is. So a level's total is just how many nodes it has.
practice.answer: Level k has 2^k nodes doing 1 unit each, so level k costs 2^k. The levels run k = 0 .. log2 n, so the total is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n = 2n - 1. Here the work doubles going down, so the n leaves dominate. T(n) = 2n - 1 = Theta(n). Check: T(2) = 3, T(4) = 7, T(8) = 15.

practice.problem: Count the inversions in [2, 4, 1, 3, 5] using merge-and-count.
practice.hint: Split as [2, 4] and [1, 3, 5]. While merging, each time you take from the right half, count the left-half elements still waiting.
practice.answer: 3 inversions: (2,1), (4,1), (4,3). For example, split into [2, 4] (0) and [1, 3, 5] (0). Merging: take 1 from the right while 2 elements remain on the left (+2); take 2; take 3 from the right while 1 remains on the left (+1); take 4, then 5. Total 3.

practice.problem: Solve each by finding the work per level. (a) T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^3. (b) T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n. (c) T(n) = T(n/2) + n.

visual.caption: Fill in each level's total work, decide who wins, and give T(n).

practice.hint: For each, write level k's total as (number of problems on level k) x (work per problem). Is it shrinking, staying the same, or growing as k goes up?
practice.answer: (a) Level k: 4^k problems of size n/2^k, each doing (n/2^k)^3, so 4^k x n^3/8^k = n^3/2^k. Shrinking by half each level, so the root wins: Theta(n^3). (b) Level k: 3^k problems of size n/3^k, each doing n/3^k, so n per level, for log3 n levels: Theta(n log n). (c) One problem per level: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n, so the root wins: Theta(n).

practice.problem: Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n.

visual.caption: 4 children per node, each half the size. What happens to the work as you go down?

practice.hint: Write level k's total: 4^k problems, each of size n/2^k. Does that grow or shrink as k goes up, and how many leaves are at the bottom?
practice.answer: Level k does 4^k x n/2^k = n 2^k work: it doubles each level, so the leaves dominate. There are 4^(log2 n) = n^(log2 4) = n^2 leaves. T(n) = Theta(n^2). (With T(1) = 1 it is exactly 2n^2 - n: T(2) = 6, T(4) = 28, T(8) = 120.)

practice.problem: (a) Multiply 57 x 34 with three single-digit-style products, Karatsuba style. (b) What would the recurrence and running time be if you used all four products ac, ad, bc, bd?
practice.hint: Split 57 into a and b, and 34 into c and d. Your three products are ac, bd and (a + b)(c + d).
practice.answer: (a) a = 5, b = 7, c = 3, d = 4. ac = 15, bd = 28, (a + b)(c + d) = 12 x 7 = 84. Middle = 84 - 15 - 28 = 41. Result 15 x 100 + 41 x 10 + 28 = 1938 (check: 57 x 34 = 1938). (b) T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n). Leaves: 4^(log2 n) = n^2, so Theta(n^2), no better than the school method.

practice.problem: A sorted array of distinct numbers was rotated, e.g. [15, 18, 22, 3, 6, 9, 12]. Give an O(log n) algorithm to find the minimum, state the invariant, and trace it on this array.

visual.caption: Mark lo, hi and mid for each round.

practice.hint: Compare A[mid] with A[hi]. If A[mid] is bigger, the drop down to the minimum must happen somewhere to the right of mid.
practice.answer: lo = 0, hi = n - 1. While lo < hi: mid = floor((lo + hi)/2); if A[mid] > A[hi], the drop is to the right of mid, so lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid. Return A[lo]. Invariant: the minimum's index is in [lo, hi]. Trace: lo 0, hi 6, mid 3: 3 <= 12, hi = 3. mid 1: 18 > 3, lo = 2. mid 2: 22 > 3, lo = 3. Answer A[3] = 3. Time T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n).

practice.problem: T(1) = 1 and T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 for n a power of 2. Guess a closed form by computing T(2), T(4), T(8), then prove it by induction.
practice.hint: Compute T(2), T(4), T(8) straight from the recurrence. Each value is one less than a power of 2. Which power, compared with n?

practice.problem: Left half (0, 4), (2, 0), (3, 7), (4, 3); right half (6, 4), (7, 0), (8, 6), (11, 3); dividing line x = 5. (a) Find delta from the halves. (b) List the strip points sorted by y. (c) Find the closest pair. (d) Why would re-sorting the strip by y in every call make the algorithm O(n log^2 n)?

visual.caption: Blue = left half, pink = right half.

practice.hint: Find the best pair inside each half first, using squared distances. delta is the smaller one; the strip is every point within delta of x = 5.
practice.answer: (a) Left best: (2, 0)-(4, 3), squared 13. Right best: (6, 4)-(8, 6), squared 8. delta = sqrt(8), about 2.83. (b) Strip 2.17 < x < 7.83: (7, 0), (4, 3), (6, 4), (3, 7). (c) (4, 3)-(6, 4), squared distance 5 (distance about 2.24), better than sqrt(8). (d) Sorting the strip costs O(n log n) per call, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n log n), which sums to O(n log^2 n). Pre-sorting by y once and splitting the sorted list in each call keeps the combine step O(n).

intro.big_idea: Break a problem into smaller overlapping questions, answer each one once, and write the answers in a table so you never solve the same thing twice. Every new cell is built from cells you already filled.
intro.picture_this: Climbing stairs 1 or 2 steps at a time: the ways to reach step 5 are the ways to reach step 4 plus the ways to reach step 3.
you_know_it_when: 'Find the best' or 'count the ways', where choices now affect choices later
A clean 'either I use this item or I don't' split
Plain recursion would solve the same small problem again and again

visual.caption: ways(5) = ways(4) + ways(3) = 5 + 3 = 8. Each cell reuses earlier cells.

problems.title: Max-weight independent set on a path
problems.problem: Nodes v1 - v2 - v3 - v4 - v5 - v6 sit on a path with weights 3, 8, 6, 2, 9, 4. Pick nodes with no two neighbors both picked, maximizing total weight. Show that 'take the heaviest node still allowed' fails, then solve it with DP and say the running time.

visual.caption: Weights are under the nodes. No two picked nodes may share an edge.

warmup.question: Path v1 - v2 - v3 with weights 2, 7, 3. Which set of non-neighboring nodes weighs the most?
warmup.answer: {v2}, weight 7. The only other real choice is {v1, v3}, which weighs just 2 + 3 = 5.

walk.say: Try greedy first: take the heaviest node, 9 (v5). That blocks v4 and v6. The heaviest left is 8 (v2), which blocks v1 and v3. Nothing is left: total 17.
walk.look: Notice: v1 and v3 (3 + 6 = 9) got blocked by v2 (8).

walk.say: Set up a table. OPT(j) = best weight using only v1 .. vj. The last node vj is either skipped, giving OPT(j - 1), or taken, giving w_j + OPT(j - 2) because v(j-1) is then blocked. OPT(0) = 0.

visual.caption: OPT(j) = max(OPT(j - 1), w_j + OPT(j - 2))

walk.say: Fill left to right. OPT(1) = 3. OPT(2) = max(3, 8 + 0) = 8. OPT(3) = max(8, 6 + 3) = 9.
walk.look: Notice: OPT(3) looked back one cell (skip) and two cells (take); take won.

walk.say: OPT(6) = max(18, 4 + 10) = 18. Skipping v6 is at least as good as taking it.
Trace back from j = 6. OPT(6) = OPT(5): skip v6. OPT(5) = 9 + OPT(3): take v5, jump to 3. OPT(3) = 6 + OPT(1): take v3, jump to 1. OPT(1) = 3: take v1.
walk.look: Notice: the teal weights are the nodes we keep.

walk.say: Answer: {v1, v3, v5}, weight 3 + 6 + 9 = 18, which beats greedy's 17. n cells with O(1) work each: O(n) time.

visual.caption: Chosen: v1, v3, v5. No two are neighbors.

problems.why: Look at the last node vj. Either the best set skips it, and then it is the best set for v1 .. v(j-1); or it uses it, and then it can't use v(j-1), so the rest must be the best set for v1 .. v(j-2). If the rest weren't best, swapping in a better one would beat the optimum. Two options per cell and n cells: O(n) time.
problems.tip: Before any numbers, write the two options in words: 'skip j' or 'take j, so skip j - 1'. The recurrence falls out of that sentence.

problems.title: Fewest coins (where greedy change fails)
problems.problem: Coins are worth 1, 3 and 4. Make 6 cents with as few coins as possible. Show the greedy rule (largest coin first) fails, then solve it with DP and give the running time.

visual.caption: Coins: 1, 3, 4. Hop from 0 to 6 in as few coins as possible.

warmup.question: With coins 1, 3 and 4, what is the fewest number of coins for 4 cents? For 3 cents? For 2 cents?
warmup.answer: 4 cents: one coin (4). 3 cents: one coin (3). 2 cents: two coins (1 + 1). Bigger amounts will reuse these small answers.

walk.say: Greedy takes the biggest coin that fits: 4, then 1, then 1. Three coins.
Subproblem: OPT(v) = fewest coins that add up to exactly v. The last coin is a 1, 3 or 4, so OPT(v) = 1 + min(OPT(v - 1), OPT(v - 3), OPT(v - 4)), skipping coins bigger than v. OPT(0) = 0.
Small amounts: OPT(1) = 1, OPT(2) = 1 + OPT(1) = 2, OPT(3) = 1 (a 3 coin), OPT(4) = 1 (a 4 coin).

walk.look: Notice: each arrow is one choice of last coin: 1, 3 or 4.

walk.say: OPT(6) = 1 + min(OPT(5), OPT(3), OPT(2)) = 1 + min(2, 1, 2) = 2. The winner is the 3 coin, which leaves OPT(3).
Answer: 2 coins, 3 + 3. With n coin types and target V the table has V cells and each tries n coins: O(nV) time.

problems.why: The optimal pile has some last coin c. Remove it and what is left must be an optimal pile for v - c. So try every coin as the last one. With n coin types and target V that is O(nV) time. Like knapsack, that is pseudo-polynomial: V can be exponential in the number of digits used to write it.
problems.tip: One counterexample kills a greedy rule; once it's dead, ask 'what was the last choice?' and that question is your recurrence.

problems.title: Weighted interval scheduling
problems.problem: Jobs (start, finish, value), sorted by finish: 1 (0, 3, 2), 2 (1, 5, 4), 3 (4, 6, 4), 4 (6, 8, 3), 5 (5, 9, 7). Find the most total value of compatible jobs.

visual.caption: Pick jobs that don't overlap, to get the most total value.

warmup.question: Job 1 runs 0-3, job 2 runs 1-5, job 3 runs 4-6. p(3) is the last job (in finish order) that ends by the time job 3 starts. What is p(3)?
warmup.answer: p(3) = 1. Job 1 ends at 3, before job 3 starts at 4. Job 2 ends at 5, so it overlaps job 3.

walk.say: Jobs are sorted by finish time. For each job j find p(j), the last job that ends by the time j starts: p = 0, 0, 1, 3, 2.
walk.look: Notice: job 5 starts at 5, and job 2 is the last one finished by then, so p(5) = 2.

walk.say: Either job j is in the best set, giving v_j + OPT(p(j)), or it isn't, giving OPT(j - 1). OPT(0) = 0. So OPT(1) = max(2 + 0, 0) = 2 and OPT(2) = max(4 + 0, 2) = 4.

walk.look: Notice: the take option jumps back to column p(3) = 1, not to column 2.

walk.say: OPT(4) = max(3 + OPT(3), OPT(3)) = max(9, 6) = 9. Here p(4) = 3, so taking job 4 keeps everything up to job 3.
Trace back. OPT(5) = 11 came from taking job 5, so jump to p(5) = 2. OPT(2) = 4 came from taking job 2 (4 + 0 beat 2), so jump to p(2) = 0. Stop.
Answer: jobs 2 and 5, total value 4 + 7 = 11. After sorting, filling the table is O(n).

problems.why: The optimal solution either uses job j or it doesn't. If it does, it can't use anything overlapping j, which leaves exactly jobs 1..p(j). If it doesn't, the answer is OPT(j - 1). Filling the table left to right takes O(n) after sorting.
problems.tip: As you fill each cell, circle which option won; tracing back the answer is then just following the circles.

problems.title: Longest increasing subsequence
problems.problem: Find a longest strictly increasing subsequence of 5, 2, 8, 6, 3, 6, 9, 7. Give the recurrence and the running time.

visual.caption: Pick numbers left to right, each bigger than the one before. How many can you get?

warmup.question: In 5, 2, 8, which numbers can come right before 8 in an increasing subsequence? How long is the longest one ending at 8?
warmup.answer: Both 5 and 2 are earlier and smaller, so either can come before 8. Length 2: 5, 8 or 2, 8.

walk.say: Define L(j) = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at a_j. Then L(j) = 1 + the biggest L(i) over earlier i with a_i < a_j (or 1 if there is none). prev(j) remembers that i.
L(1) = 1 and L(2) = 1 (nothing smaller comes before 2). L(3): 8 can follow 5 or 2, both with L = 1, so L(3) = 2 with prev 1 (keep the earliest on a tie).
L(4): 6 can follow 5 or 2, so L = 2, prev 1. L(5): 3 can only follow 2, so L = 2, prev 2.
L(6): 6 can follow 5, 2 or 3. The best of those is a5 = 3 with L = 2, so L(6) = 3, prev 5.
walk.look: Notice: 8 and 6 come earlier but are not smaller than 6, so they are not allowed.

walk.say: L(7): 9 can follow anything before it. The best is a6 = 6 with L = 3, so L(7) = 4. L(8): 7 can also follow a6, so L(8) = 4.
The answer is the biggest L anywhere: 4. Follow prev back from j = 7: 9, then a6 = 6, a5 = 3, a2 = 2. So 2, 3, 6, 9. Each j scans all earlier i: O(n^2).

visual.caption: Teal: 2, 3, 6, 9 (7 instead of 9 also works).

walk.look: Notice: the best subsequence need not end at the last element.

problems.why: Fixing where the subsequence ends makes the subproblem clean: the element before a_j is some smaller a_i, and the part ending at a_i must itself be as long as possible. Each j scans all earlier i, so O(n^2) time. The answer is the max over every L(j), not L(n), because the best subsequence need not end at the last element.
problems.tip: Define the subproblem as 'ending exactly at j'. Without the word 'exactly' you can't tell which earlier values are allowed to come before a_j.

problems.title: Segmented least squares
problems.problem: Points p1 .. p5 are sorted by x. e(i, j) is the error of the best single line through p_i .. p_j: e(1,3) = 1, e(1,4) = 6, e(1,5) = 12, e(2,4) = 4, e(2,5) = 9, e(3,5) = 2, and every e(i, j) with j - i <= 1 is 0. Each line costs C = 3. Split the points into consecutive segments to minimize (total error) + C x (number of lines).

visual.caption: e(i, j): error of the best single line through p_i .. p_j. Row = first point, column = last point.

warmup.question: One line through p1, p2, p3 has error 1. Two lines (p1-p2 and p3 alone) have error 0. With C = 3 per line, which is cheaper?
warmup.answer: One line: 1 + 3 = 4. Two lines: 0 + 3 + 3 = 6. One line wins, because C is the price of every extra line.

walk.say: OPT(j) = cheapest cost for p1 .. pj. The last segment is p_i .. p_j for some i, so OPT(j) = min over 1 <= i <= j of e(i, j) + C + OPT(i - 1). OPT(0) = 0.
OPT(1) = 0 + 3 + 0 = 3. OPT(2) = min(0 + 3 + 0, 0 + 3 + 3) = 3: one line through p1 and p2.
OPT(3) = min(1 + 3 + 0, 0 + 3 + 3, 0 + 3 + 3) = 4, with i = 1: one line through p1 .. p3.
walk.look: Notice: i = 1 means the last segment starts at p1, so it adds OPT(0).

walk.say: Trace back: OPT(5) used p4 .. p5, then OPT(3) used p1 .. p3. Two lines, cost (1 + 0) + 2 x 3 = 7. Each OPT(j) tries j starts: O(n^2) once the e(i, j) are known.

problems.why: The last point p_n belongs to exactly one segment, which starts at some p_i. Once you pick i, you pay that segment's error and its C, and the points before it are an independent smaller problem. Trying all i costs O(n) per cell, so O(n^2) for the DP once the e(i, j) values are known.
problems.tip: C is the price of a new line: a big C pushes toward one long line, a tiny C toward many short ones. Sanity-check your answer against that.

problems.title: 0/1 knapsack
problems.problem: Capacity W = 5. Items (weight, value): A (2, 3), B (3, 4), C (4, 5), D (5, 6). Find the best total value.

visual.caption: Which items fit in a bag of capacity 5 for the most value?

warmup.question: Capacity 5. Item A weighs 2 (value 3), item B weighs 3 (value 4). Can you take both? What is the best value?
warmup.answer: Yes: 2 + 3 = 5 fits exactly, for value 3 + 4 = 7. Every cell of the table asks this kind of question.

walk.say: OPT(i, w) = best value using the first i items with capacity w. The row 'none' is all 0. Each cell either skips item i (look straight up) or takes it (v_i + the cell one row up and w_i columns left).
Row A (2, 3): A fits once w >= 2, so the row is 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3.
Row B (3, 4): at w = 3, max(3, 4 + OPT(A, 0)) = 4. At w = 5, max(skip: 3, take: 4 + OPT(A, 2) = 7) = 7.
walk.look: Notice: the take arrow comes from 3 columns left, because B weighs 3.

walk.say: Row C (4, 5): at w = 4, max(4, 5 + 0) = 5. At w = 5, max(skip: 7, take: 5 + OPT(B, 1) = 5) = 7.
Row D (5, 6): D only fits at w = 5, where max(skip: 7, take: 6 + OPT(C, 0) = 6) = 7. Everywhere else, copy the row above.
Trace back from the bottom-right 7. Rows D and C: the 7 came from above, so skip them. Row B: the 7 came from 4 + OPT(A, 2), so take B and move to w = 2. Row A: 3 = 3 + OPT(none, 0), so take A.

visual.caption: Teal = items taken (B, then A).

walk.look: Notice: the trace moves left only when an item is taken.

walk.say: Answer: take A and B, weight 5, value 7. The table has (n + 1)(W + 1) cells with O(1) work each: O(nW) time, which is pseudo-polynomial.

visual.caption: Weight 2 + 3 = 5, value 3 + 4 = 7.

problems.why: Greedy by value per weight fails in general, so you need a subproblem that remembers remaining capacity. The table is n x W, so the time is O(nW). That is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the number W, not on how many bits it takes to write W.
problems.tip: Each cell asks: is this item worth the space it takes? Look straight up (skip it) or up and left by its weight (take it).

problems.title: Sequence alignment (edit distance)
problems.problem: Align X = lamp with Y = palm. A gap costs delta = 2, a mismatched pair costs alpha = 3, a matching pair costs 0. Find the cheapest alignment and its cost.

visual.caption: Line the words up, using gaps (-) where needed. Gap 2, mismatch 3, match 0.

warmup.question: Align an with na (gap 2, mismatch 3). Which is cheaper: a/n + n/a (two mismatches), or -/n, a/a, n/- (two gaps around a match)?
warmup.answer: Two mismatches cost 3 + 3 = 6. Two gaps around the matching a cost 2 + 0 + 2 = 4. The gaps win.

walk.say: OPT(i, j) = cheapest alignment of the first i letters of lamp with the first j letters of palm. Lining letters up against nothing costs 2 each, so the gap row and column are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
Each cell is the min of three: diagonal + (0 if the letters match, else 3), up + 2, left + 2. Row l: OPT(1, 1) = min(0 + 3, 2 + 2, 2 + 2) = 3, and the row is 3, 5, 4, 6.
walk.look: Notice: the 4 is l matched with l: diagonal 4 + 0.

walk.say: Row a: OPT(2, 2) pairs a with a for free: 0 + OPT(1, 1) = 3. The row is 5, 3, 5, 7.
Row m: 7, 5, 6, 5. OPT(3, 4) pairs m with m for free: 0 + OPT(2, 3) = 5.
Row p: 6, 7, 8, 7. The corner OPT(4, 4) = min(3 + 6, 2 + 5, 2 + 8) = 7, coming from above: the final p of lamp sits against a gap.
Trace back from the corner: up (p/-), diagonal (m/m), left (-/l), diagonal (a/a), diagonal (l/p).
walk.look: Notice: diagonal = two letters paired, sideways or down = a gap.

walk.say: Answer: cost 7 = 3 (l/p) + 0 (a/a) + 2 (-/l) + 0 (m/m) + 2 (p/-). The table has (m + 1)(n + 1) cells with O(1) work each: O(mn).

problems.why: The last column of any alignment is one of three things: x_i paired with y_j, x_i against a gap, or y_j against a gap. Whatever is left is a smaller alignment problem, and it must be solved optimally. The table is (m + 1) x (n + 1) with O(1) work per cell, so O(mn) time and space.
problems.tip: Fill the gap row and gap column first (0, 2, 4, 6, ...); every other cell then needs only its left, up and diagonal neighbors.

problems.title: Bellman-Ford with a negative edge
problems.problem: Edges: s->a 4, s->b 5, b->a -3, a->t 2. No negative cycles. Find the shortest s to t distance.

visual.caption: One negative edge (coral). Find the shortest distance from s to t.

warmup.question: Edges s->a 4, s->b 5, b->a -3. Which is the cheaper way to reach a: straight there, or through b?
warmup.answer: Through b: 5 - 3 = 2, which beats 4. A negative edge can make a longer path cheaper, which is why Dijkstra can go wrong here.

walk.say: OPT(i, v) = shortest s-to-v distance using at most i edges. Round 0: s = 0, everything else is infinity.
Round 1 (paths of one edge): a = 4 and b = 5. t needs at least two edges, so it stays infinity.

walk.look: Notice: a dropped from 4 to 2 by going through b.

walk.say: Round 3: t = OPT(2, a) + 2 = 2 + 2 = 4. Nothing else changes.
Here n = 4, so n - 1 = 3 rounds are enough: with no negative cycles, a shortest path never repeats a node and has at most 3 edges. One row per round keeps it tidy.
Answer: 4, along s -> b -> a -> t. Dijkstra would settle a at 4 before ever looking at the -3 edge, and report t = 6.

problems.why: With no negative cycles, a shortest path never repeats a node, so it has at most n - 1 edges. Building answers for 'at most i edges' for i = 1 .. n - 1 therefore reaches the true distances, in O(mn) time.
problems.tip: Bellman-Ford is just 'relax every edge' repeated n - 1 times; one row per round keeps it tidy.

problems.title: Bellman-Ford: detecting a negative cycle
problems.problem: Edges: s->a 2, a->b 1, b->c -3, c->a 1, c->t 2 (n = 5 nodes). Run Bellman-Ford from s for n rounds, one row per round. Is there a negative cycle reachable from s? Explain why the extra round tells you.

visual.caption: n = 5 nodes. Is there a cycle whose total weight is negative?

warmup.question: A cycle a -> b -> c -> a has edge weights 1, -3 and 1. What is its total? What happens if you keep going around it?
warmup.answer: 1 - 3 + 1 = -1. Every lap lowers the distance by 1 more, so no shortest walk exists: it heads to minus infinity.

walk.say: Round i uses only the previous row: d_i(v) = min(d_(i-1)(v), d_(i-1)(u) + w(u, v)) over every edge u->v. Round 1: a = 0 + 2 = 2.
Round 2: b = 2 + 1 = 3. Round 3: c = 3 - 3 = 0.
Round 4 (= n - 1): a = min(2, c + 1) = 1 and t = c + 2 = 2. With no negative cycle, these would be final.
Round 5 (= n), the extra round: b = min(3, a + 1) = 2. Something still changed!
walk.look: Notice: compare rows 4 and 5. Only b moved, from 3 to 2.

walk.say: So a negative cycle is reachable from s: a -> b -> c -> a weighs 1 - 3 + 1 = -1. Following prev pointers back from b walks around it.

visual.caption: The coral cycle has total weight -1.

walk.say: Why one extra round is the test: without a negative cycle, a shortest walk never repeats a node, so it uses at most n - 1 edges and round n changes nothing. Each round relaxes all m edges: O(mn).

visual.caption: Any change in round n means a negative cycle.

problems.why: With no negative cycle, a shortest walk never needs to repeat a node, so it uses at most n - 1 edges and round n changes nothing. If round n does improve some d(v), the best walk to v with n edges has n + 1 node visits, so it repeats a node; the loop between the repeats must be negative, or cutting it out would give a walk with fewer edges that is no longer. Each round relaxes all m edges: O(mn) total.
problems.tip: Run exactly one extra round and compare rows. 'Did anything change in round n?' is the whole negative-cycle test.

problems.title: Design a DP from scratch: hotel stops
problems.problem: You drive along a road from mile 0 and must end at the last hotel. Hotels are at miles a1 < a2 < ... < an. You stop only at hotels, and a day of x miles costs (200 - x)^2. Design an algorithm for the cheapest trip, prove it correct, give the running time, and run it on hotels at 150, 220, 400, 600.

visual.caption: Hotels at 150, 220, 400 and 600. A day of x miles costs (200 - x)^2.

warmup.question: A day of x miles costs (200 - x)^2. What does a 150-mile day cost? A 220-mile day?
warmup.answer: (200 - 150)^2 = 2500 and (200 - 220)^2 = 400. Being 50 miles off costs far more than being 20 off.

walk.say: Subproblem: OPT(j) = least total penalty for a trip that ends its last day at hotel j. Add home as stop 0 at mile 0, with OPT(0) = 0.
Recurrence: the last day starts at some earlier stop i, so OPT(j) = min over i < j of OPT(i) + (200 - (a_j - a_i))^2. Fill j = 1, 2, ..., n; the answer is OPT(n).

visual.caption: One choice for j = 3: a best trip to 220, then a last day of 180 miles.

walk.look: Notice: 400 to 600 is exactly 200 miles, so that last day is free.

walk.say: Trace the 'from' row back: 4 <- 3 <- 2 <- 0. Stop at 220, 400 and 600. Penalties 400 + 400 + 0 = 800.

Correctness, by induction on j: the best trip to j has some last stop i. Its part up to i must be a best trip to i, or swapping in a better one would make the whole trip cheaper. So the min sees the best trip.
Time: hotel j checks j earlier stops, so 1 + 2 + ... + n = O(n^2) time and O(n) space.

problems.why: A full-credit 'design a DP' answer names the subproblem in words, gives the recurrence with base case, says the fill order and where the answer is, argues the recurrence is right (the last choice plus an optimal rest), and counts the time as (number of cells) x (work per cell). Greedy 'drive as close to 200 as you can each day' is a tempting wrong answer.
problems.tip: Write the five parts as headers on your exam page (subproblem, recurrence, order and answer, correctness, time) and fill each in; graders look for every one.

problems.title: RNA secondary structure: a DP over intervals
problems.problem: An RNA strand b_1 ... b_n folds by pairing bases. Rules: only A-U and C-G pair; each base is in at most one pair; no sharp turns (a pair (i, j) needs i < j - 4); pairs don't cross (if (i, j) and (k, l) are pairs with i < k, then not i < k < j < l). Find the most pairs for GCAUUUAGC (n = 9). Give the recurrence, explain why one index isn't enough, and give the running time.

visual.caption: A-U and C-G can pair. Pairs can't cross, and a pair (i, j) needs i < j - 4.

warmup.question: Ignore the letters. Could bases 1 and 5 form a pair under the rule i < j - 4? What about 1 and 6?
warmup.answer: 1 and 5: is 1 < 1? No, too sharp a turn. 1 and 6: 1 < 2, yes. A pair needs at least 4 bases strictly between its ends.

walk.say: OPT(i, j) = most pairs using only b_i .. b_j. If j - i <= 4, no pair fits inside, so OPT(i, j) = 0. For example OPT(3, 7) = 0: A U U U A is too short to fold.

Two cases for the last base b_j. Either it stays unpaired: OPT(i, j - 1). Or it pairs with some b_t (complementary, t < j - 4), which splits the rest into an outside piece OPT(i, t - 1) and an inside piece OPT(t + 1, j - 1).

visual.caption: Pairing b_8 with b_2: nothing can cross the arc, so inside and outside are separate.

walk.look: Notice: the inside piece starts at t + 1, not at 1. That's why we need intervals, not prefixes.

walk.say: Fill the table by interval length, shortest first. Every interval with j - i <= 4 is 0. The j - i = 5 intervals are 0 too: only their two ends could pair, and none of those end pairs is complementary.
walk.look: Notice: rows are the start i, columns the end j. The faded lower half is unused.

walk.say: OPT(2, 8): b_8 = G can pair with the C at t = 2, since 2 < 8 - 4. Inside is OPT(3, 7) = 0. So OPT(2, 8) = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1.
OPT(1, 9): b_9 = C can pair with the G at t = 1 (the G at t = 8 is too close). That gives 1 + OPT(2, 8) = 2, which beats leaving C unpaired, OPT(1, 8) = 1.
Answer: 2 pairs, (1, 9) G-C and (2, 8) C-G, nested and not crossing. The full table shows OPT(1, 9) = 2 in the corner.
walk.look: Notice: the pink cell OPT(2, 8) = 1 feeds the corner.

walk.say: Time: there are O(n^2) intervals, and each tries O(n) partners t for b_j. Total O(n^3).

visual.caption: O(n^2) cells x O(n) choices = O(n^3).

problems.why: A prefix OPT(j) isn't enough: pairing b_j with b_t splits the problem into the part before t and the part strictly between t and j, and the inside part is an interval that doesn't start at 1. When one choice cuts the input into an 'outside' and an 'inside', use intervals OPT(i, j) and fill them shortest first, so every piece you need is already in the table.
problems.tip: Write the two cases as 'b_j unpaired' and 'b_j paired with t'. Then check t's range: the no-sharp-turn rule is the easiest thing to forget.

practice.problem: Path weights v1 .. v6 = 4, 5, 4, 1, 6, 3. (a) What does 'take the heaviest allowed node' give? (b) Fill OPT(j) and find the best independent set.
practice.hint: For (b), fill OPT left to right with OPT(j) = max(OPT(j - 1), w_j + OPT(j - 2)), starting from OPT(0) = 0 and OPT(1) = 4.
practice.answer: (a) Greedy takes 6 (v5), then 5 (v2); everything else is blocked, total 11. (b) OPT(1) = 4, OPT(2) = max(4, 5) = 5, OPT(3) = max(5, 4 + 4) = 8, OPT(4) = max(8, 1 + 5) = 8, OPT(5) = max(8, 6 + 8) = 14, OPT(6) = max(14, 3 + 8) = 14. Trace back: skip v6, take v5, then OPT(3) takes v3, then v1. Best set {v1, v3, v5}, weight 14.

practice.problem: Coins 1, 5, 6, 9. Make 11 cents with the fewest coins. What does greedy give? Fill OPT(0) .. OPT(11).
practice.hint: Fill upward from OPT(0) = 0. For each v, try each coin c <= v as the last coin and take 1 + the smallest OPT(v - c).

practice.problem: Weighted interval scheduling, sorted by finish (start, finish, value): 1 (0, 2, 3), 2 (1, 4, 5), 3 (3, 5, 4), 4 (2, 6, 6), 5 (5, 7, 2). Find p(j), fill OPT(j), and list the jobs.
practice.hint: First find p(j) for each job: the last job that finishes by the time job j starts. Then fill OPT left to right.

practice.problem: Find a longest strictly increasing subsequence of 4, 1, 7, 3, 5, 2, 6. Fill L(j) and prev(j).
practice.hint: Work left to right. For each j, look back at every earlier value smaller than a_j and take the one with the biggest L.
practice.answer: L = 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4. prev (earliest i on ties): a3 = 7 after a1, a4 = 3 after a2, a5 = 5 after a4, a6 = 2 after a2, a7 = 6 after a5. Longest length 4: 1, 3, 5, 6. O(n^2) time.

visual.caption: The error table e(i, j). Row = first point, column = last point.

practice.hint: Compute OPT(1), OPT(2), ... in order. For each j, try every start i of the last segment: e(i, j) + C + OPT(i - 1).
practice.answer: OPT(1) = 2, OPT(2) = 2, OPT(3) = 4, OPT(4) = 4, OPT(5) = 6, OPT(6) = 6. For OPT(6): i = 5 gives 0 + 2 + OPT(4) = 6, i = 4 gives 1 + 2 + OPT(3) = 7, smaller i cost more. Trace back: p5..p6, then OPT(4) uses p3..p4, then OPT(2) uses p1..p2. Three lines, zero error, cost 3 x 2 = 6.

practice.problem: 0/1 knapsack with W = 6. Items (weight, value): A (1, 1), B (2, 6), C (3, 10), D (5, 15).
practice.hint: Fill row by row. In each cell compare skip (straight up) with take (the item's value + the cell one row up and its weight to the left).
practice.answer: Best is 17, using A + B + C (weight 6). Compare: B + C = 16, D + A = 16, D alone = 15. Table rows (w = 0 .. 6): none 0 0 0 0 0 0 0; A 0 1 1 1 1 1 1; B 0 1 6 7 7 7 7; C 0 1 6 10 11 16 17; D 0 1 6 10 11 16 17.

practice.problem: Align X = tame with Y = team. Gap delta = 2, mismatch alpha = 3, match 0. Fill the table and give the cheapest alignment.
practice.hint: The gap row and column are already filled. Each other cell is the min of: diagonal + (0 or 3), up + 2, left + 2.
practice.answer: Rows (tame) x columns (team): row 0: 0 2 4 6 8; t: 2 0 2 4 6; a: 4 2 3 2 4; m: 6 4 5 4 2; e: 8 6 4 6 4. Cost 4: t/t, -/e, a/a, m/m, e/-. Two gaps (2 + 2) beat any mismatches; pairing letters straight across would cost 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.

practice.problem: Bellman-Ford from s. Edges: s->a 3, s->b 4, b->a -2, a->c 2, b->c 4, c->t 1.
practice.hint: Make a table with one row per round. Each round uses only the previous row: d_i(v) = min(d_(i-1)(v), d_(i-1)(u) + w(u, v)) over edges u->v.
practice.answer: i=1: a 3, b 4. i=2: a 2, c 5. i=3: c 4, t 6. i=4: t 5. Shortest distance to t is 5, along s -> b -> a -> c -> t.

practice.problem: Edges: s->a 4, s->c 6, a->b -2, b->c 3, c->a 1, c->t -1 (n = 5). Run 5 rounds of Bellman-Ford from s. Is there a negative cycle? What is d(t)?
practice.hint: Keep one row per round, using only the previous row. After round 5, compare it with round 4: any change means a negative cycle.
practice.answer: Round 1: a 4, c 6. Round 2: b 2, t 5. Round 3: c 5. Round 4: t 4. Round 5: no change, so no negative cycle (a -> b -> c -> a weighs -2 + 3 + 1 = 2). d(t) = 4 along s -> a -> b -> c -> t: 4 - 2 + 3 - 1.

practice.problem: Pretty printing. Words have lengths w1 .. wn and a line holds L characters. A line with words i .. j uses w_i + ... + w_j + (j - i) characters (one space between words) and costs (L - used)^2; every line counts, the last one too. Design a DP for the cheapest layout and run it on lengths 3, 4, 2, 5 with L = 10.

visual.caption: L = 10. A line with words i .. j uses their lengths plus (j - i) spaces.

practice.hint: OPT(j) = cheapest layout of words 1 .. j. The last line holds words i .. j: try each i whose words fit in 10 characters.
practice.answer: OPT(j) = cheapest layout of words 1 .. j. OPT(j) = min over i with words i .. j fitting of OPT(i - 1) + (L - used(i, j))^2, OPT(0) = 0. Order j = 1 .. n, answer OPT(n). Correct for the same reason: the last line holds words i .. j, and the lines before it must be laid out optimally. Time O(n^2) with prefix sums for used(i, j). Run: OPT(1) = 7^2 = 49. OPT(2) = (10 - 8)^2 = 4 (words 1-2 on one line). OPT(3) = min(49 + (10 - 7)^2, 4 + (10 - 2)^2) = 58 (words 1-3 don't fit on one line). OPT(4) = min(4 + (10 - 8)^2, 58 + (10 - 5)^2) = 8. Layout: [3 4] [2 5], cost 4 + 4 = 8.

practice.problem: Use the same rules and recurrence on GACUUCAGUC (n = 10). Find the most pairs and list them. Which subproblems does pairing b_10 with b_1 leave?

visual.caption: Draw arcs for the pairs. Remember i < j - 4.

practice.hint: Work from the outside in. Can b_10 = C pair with b_1 = G? If so, ask the same question about the inside interval, and keep going.
practice.answer: 3 pairs: (1, 10) G-C, (2, 9) A-U, (3, 8) C-G, nested inside each other. Pairing b_10 with b_1 leaves OPT(1, 0) = 0 (nothing before t = 1) and OPT(2, 9). Inside, (2, 9) leaves OPT(3, 8), and (3, 8) is allowed because 3 < 8 - 4. Nothing fits inside (4, 7). OPT(1, 10) = 3.

intro.big_idea: Push as much 'stuff' as you can from a source s to a sink t through pipes with capacities. Keep finding a path with spare room and push more along it; when no such path is left, you're at the max.
intro.picture_this: Water through pipes or cars through roads: the skinniest set of pipes you'd have to cut to separate s from t is exactly what limits the whole flow.
you_know_it_when: Edges with capacities or limits, plus a source and a sink
Assignments where each person or slot is used at most once
'How much can get through?' or 'what's the cheapest way to cut it apart?'

visual.caption: Each pipe shows flow / capacity. Here 3 units make it from s to t.

problems.title: Ford-Fulkerson by hand
problems.problem: Capacities: s->a 3, s->b 2, a->b 1, a->t 2, b->t 3. Find a max flow and a matching min cut.

visual.caption: Each number is a pipe's capacity. Nothing is flowing yet.

warmup.question: A path from s to t has edges with room 4, 1 and 3 left. How much can you push along the whole path?
warmup.answer: 1. A path can only carry what its tightest edge allows, so you push the bottleneck: min(4, 1, 3) = 1.

visual.caption: room left on each edge

walk.say: Write used/capacity on every edge. Nothing flows yet, so every label starts at 0.

visual.caption: value 0

walk.look: Notice: the room left on an edge is capacity minus used, so right now every edge has full room.

walk.say: Pick any path with room: s -> a -> t. Its rooms are 3 and 2, so the bottleneck is 2. Push 2.

visual.caption: value 2

walk.look: Notice: a->t now reads 2/2. It is full, so no later path can use it forward.

walk.say: Next path: s -> b -> t with rooms 2 and 3. Bottleneck 2. Push 2.

visual.caption: value 4

walk.look: Notice: s->b is now full too. Only s->a still has room out of s.

walk.say: Look for leftover room: s->a has 1, a->b has 1, b->t has 1. Push 1 along the zig-zag s -> a -> b -> t.

visual.caption: value 5

walk.look: Notice: the middle edge a->b lets a's extra unit reach t through b.

walk.say: Both edges out of s are full, so s can reach nothing new. The cut A = {s} has capacity 3 + 2 = 5, equal to the flow.
walk.look: Notice: the two coral edges are the only ones leaving A, and both are full.

walk.say: Answer: max flow 5 (2 on s->a->t, 2 on s->b->t, 1 on s->a->b->t). Min cut A = {s}, B = {a, b, t}, capacity 5. Flow = cut, so both are optimal.

visual.caption: max flow 5 = min cut 5

walk.look: Notice: every label is now a final answer you could hand in.

problems.why: Each push raises the flow by the bottleneck and never breaks a capacity. When no path with room is left, the nodes s can still reach form a cut whose edges are all full, so the flow equals that cut's capacity. No flow can beat any cut, so this flow is maximum and the cut is minimum.
problems.tip: Write used/capacity on every edge and keep a running 'value' total. Finish by naming a cut with the same number.

problems.title: Build the residual graph
problems.problem: Capacities: s->a 4, s->b 2, a->b 3, a->t 1, b->t 5. Current flow: s->a 3, s->b 2, a->b 2, a->t 1, b->t 4 (value 5). Draw the residual graph, find an augmenting path, and push along it.

visual.caption: flow / capacity, value 5

warmup.question: An edge u->v has capacity 5 and carries 3. In the residual graph it becomes two edges. Which directions, and how much room on each?
warmup.answer: u->v with room 5 - 3 = 2 (you can add 2 more), and v->u with room 3 (you can undo up to the 3 already sent).

walk.say: Rule: an edge with flow f and capacity c becomes a forward edge with room c - f and a backward edge with room f. Skip any edge whose room is 0. Start with s->a (3/4): forward 1, backward 3.
walk.look: Notice: the dashed coral arrow points backward, from a to s. It means 'take back up to 3'.

walk.say: s->b is 2/2, full: no forward edge, only backward b->s with room 2. a->b is 2/3: forward 1, backward 2.
walk.look: Notice: a full edge leaves only its backward arrow behind.

walk.say: a->t is 1/1, full: only backward t->a 1. b->t is 4/5: forward 1, backward 4. The residual graph is complete.
walk.look: Notice: blue arrows are ways to add flow, coral ones are ways to cancel flow.

walk.say: Search from s using only residual arrows. s->a (1), a->b (1), b->t (1) reaches t. That is an augmenting path with bottleneck 1.
walk.look: Notice: the highlighted path uses only forward arrows here, each with room 1.

walk.say: Push 1 along s -> a -> b -> t back in the real graph: s->a 4/4, a->b 3/3, b->t 5/5. The value is now 6.

visual.caption: value 6

walk.look: Notice: three edges just became full.

walk.say: Answer: the new flow has value 6. Both edges out of s are full, so the cut A = {s} has capacity 4 + 2 = 6 = the flow, and no augmenting path is left. It is a max flow.

visual.caption: flow 6 = cut {s} 6

walk.look: Notice: with no room out of s, the residual graph can't even leave s.

problems.why: The residual graph lists every legal change to the flow: forward edges add flow where there is room, backward edges cancel flow an earlier path sent the wrong way. A path from s to t in it can always be pushed without breaking any capacity or conservation, and when none exists the flow is maximum. With integer capacities each push adds at least 1, so Ford-Fulkerson takes O(mC) time, where C is the capacity out of s.
problems.tip: Draw each original edge as a pair: room left forward, flow so far backward. A full edge has no forward arrow; an empty edge has no backward arrow.

problems.title: Read the min cut off the residual graph
problems.problem: Capacities: s->a 5, s->b 4, a->b 2, a->c 2, b->c 3, b->d 2, c->t 4, d->t 4. Ford-Fulkerson ends with flow s->a 2, s->b 4, a->b 0, a->c 2, b->c 2, b->d 2, c->t 4, d->t 2. Find the min cut and check it against the flow value.

visual.caption: final flow / capacity

warmup.question: A = {s, x}, B = {t}. Edges: s->x 5, x->t 2, t->x 9. What is the capacity of this cut?
warmup.answer: 2. Only edges going from A to B count, and that is just x->t. The 9 on t->x points back into A, so it is ignored.

walk.say: First the flow value: what leaves s. s->a carries 2 and s->b carries 4, so the value is 6.

visual.caption: value 2 + 4 = 6

walk.look: Notice: s->b is 4/4, already full.

walk.say: Now grow A = the nodes s can reach in the residual graph. s->a has room 3, so a joins. s->b is full, so it gives nothing.
walk.look: Notice: we only step along edges with room left (or backward along edges with flow).

walk.say: From a: a->b is 0/2, room 2, so b joins. a->c is 2/2, full.
walk.look: Notice: b got in through a, even though s->b itself is full.

walk.say: From b: b->c is 2/3, room 1, so c joins. b->d is 2/2, full.
walk.look: Notice: d is still outside, because the only way in is full.

walk.say: From c: c->t is 4/4, full. Its backward edges lead to a and b, already in A. Nothing new, so stop: A = {s, a, b, c}, B = {d, t}.
walk.look: Notice: both coral edges leave A, and both are full.

walk.say: Answer: min cut A = {s, a, b, c}, B = {d, t}. Edges from A to B: b->d 2 + c->t 4 = 6. That equals the flow value 6, so the flow is maximum and the cut is minimum.

visual.caption: cut capacity 2 + 4 = 6

walk.look: Notice: for the capacity we read capacities, not flows, of the edges leaving A.

problems.why: When Ford-Fulkerson stops, t is not reachable from s in the residual graph. Let A be what s can reach. Every edge leaving A must be full (or its forward residual edge would reach farther) and every edge entering A must carry 0 (or its backward residual edge would). So the flow across the cut equals its capacity, and since no flow beats any cut, both are optimal.
problems.tip: Only edges going from A to B count toward a cut's capacity. Edges going from B back into A are ignored, even if they are huge.

problems.title: Bipartite matching as flow
problems.problem: Students 1, 2, 3 and projects x, y, z. Allowed pairs: 1-x, 1-y, 2-x, 3-x. Each student gets at most one project and each project at most one student. Find a maximum matching using flow.

warmup.question: Students 1 and 2 both want only project x, and x can take one student. How many of them can be matched?
warmup.answer: Just 1. Whoever gets x uses it up, so the other has nothing left.

walk.say: Build a network: s -> each student, each allowed pair student -> project, each project -> t. Every edge gets capacity 1, so each student and project is used at most once.
walk.look: Notice: one unit of flow from s to t is exactly one student paired with one project.

walk.say: Push 1 along s -> 1 -> x -> t. Now student 1 is matched to x.

visual.caption: matching {1-x}, value 1

walk.look: Notice: x->t is full, so no one else can reach t through x directly.

walk.say: Student 2 only wants x, which is taken. In the residual graph go s -> 2 -> x, then backward x -> 1 (undo 1-x), then 1 -> y -> t. Bottleneck 1.

visual.caption: augmenting path uses a backward edge

walk.look: Notice: the coral dashed edge is the undo. Student 1 moves over to y to make room.

walk.say: After the push: 1-y and 2-x are matched, value 2. Student 3 also wants only x. Search from s: s -> 3 -> x -> (undo) 2, and 2 has nowhere else to go. t is unreachable.

visual.caption: value 2; yellow = reachable from s

walk.look: Notice: the yellow nodes are everything s can still reach. t is not among them.

walk.say: The reachable set gives a cut: only s->1 and x->t leave it, capacity 2. So no flow, and no matching, can be bigger than 2.

visual.caption: cut: s->1 + x->t = 2

walk.look: Notice: the coral edges leave the yellow set. In matching words, students 2 and 3 share the single project x.

walk.say: Answer: maximum matching {1-y, 2-x}, size 2. One of students 2 and 3 must go without, since both depend on x.
walk.look: Notice: matched pairs are exactly the middle edges carrying flow 1.

problems.why: Capacity 1 into each student and out of each project means an integer flow uses each one at most once, so integer flows and matchings are the same thing, with flow value = matching size. Ford-Fulkerson finds an integer max flow, which is a maximum matching, in O(mn) time since the value is at most n.
problems.tip: Whenever something can be used 'at most once', give it capacity 1 and let flow do the bookkeeping. Backward edges are how a student gets 'moved' to make room.

problems.title: Edge-disjoint paths as flow
problems.problem: Directed edges: s->a, s->b, s->c, a->b, b->c, a->x, c->y, x->z, x->t, y->z, y->t, z->t. Find the most s-t paths that share no edge, and prove no more exist.

warmup.question: Paths s -> a -> t and s -> a -> b -> t. Are they edge-disjoint? Do they share a node?
warmup.answer: Not edge-disjoint: both use the edge s->a. They share node a too, but sharing a node is allowed; sharing an edge is not.

walk.say: Give every edge capacity 1. Then one unit of flow is one path, and two units can never squeeze through the same edge.

visual.caption: every edge has capacity 1

walk.look: Notice: s has 3 edges out, so 3 is the most we could hope for.

walk.say: Path 1: s -> a -> x -> t. Push 1 unit along it.

visual.caption: 1 path

walk.look: Notice: the teal edges are used up now.

walk.say: Path 2: s -> c -> y -> t. It uses none of path 1's edges. Push 1.

visual.caption: 2 paths

walk.look: Notice: s->b is still free, but where can b go?

walk.say: Try a third. From b you can only reach c, and everything from {s, a, b, c} to the right side goes through a->x or c->y. Both are used.
walk.look: Notice: only two arrows cross out of the yellow blob.

walk.say: Delete those two edges and t is cut off from s. So any set of edge-disjoint paths has at most 2 paths: each needs its own crossing edge.

visual.caption: cut of 2 edges

walk.look: Notice: this cut has capacity 2, the same as our flow.

walk.say: Answer: 2 edge-disjoint paths, s -> a -> x -> t and s -> c -> y -> t. The cut {a->x, c->y} proves no third path exists.

visual.caption: 2 paths, 2 cut edges

walk.look: Notice: a matching pair (k paths, k cut edges) is a complete proof.

problems.why: k edge-disjoint paths give a flow of value k, one unit per path. An integer flow of value k gives k paths: walk from s along edges carrying 1, remove that path, repeat. So the max number of edge-disjoint paths equals the max flow, which equals the min cut: the fewest edges whose removal separates t from s (Menger's theorem).
problems.tip: To prove 'no more paths', name a set of k edges whose removal cuts s from t. k paths plus k cut edges is a complete answer.

problems.title: Node capacities by splitting nodes
problems.problem: Capacities: s->a 5, s->b 5, a->c 5, b->c 5, a->t 2, b->t 1, c->t 10. A router c can forward at most 4 units in total. Model the node limit and find the max flow.
