walk.say: Answer: E[X] = 7k/8. A random variable can't always be below its average, so some assignment satisfies at least 7k/8 clauses.

visual.caption: k = 8: some assignment satisfies 7 or 8

walk.look: Notice: if every assignment scored below 7, the average would be below 7 too.

problems.why: Linearity of expectation adds up each clause's chance separately, even though clauses share variables and so depend on each other. And since a random variable is at least its average with positive probability, an expected value proves a good assignment exists.
problems.tip: Linearity of expectation: add up each clause's chance separately; you never have to worry about how clauses overlap.

problems.title: Expected fixed points by linearity
problems.problem: n people check their hats, and the hats are handed back in a uniformly random order. What is the expected number of people who get their own hat? Check it by hand for n = 3.

visual.caption: Order 132: person 1 gets hat 1, person 2 gets hat 3, person 3 gets hat 2.

warmup.question: A 0/1 variable X equals 1 with probability 0.3 and 0 otherwise. What is E[X]?
warmup.answer: E[X] = 1 × 0.3 + 0 × 0.7 = 0.3. For a 0/1 variable, the expected value is just the chance it is 1.

walk.say: Brute force first, for n = 3. List all 6 orders and count how many people get their own hat in each: 3, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1. Total 6, so the average is 6/6 = 1.

visual.caption: average = 6/6 = 1

walk.look: Notice: this works for n = 3 but listing n! orders is hopeless for big n.

walk.say: Smarter: split the count into 0/1 pieces. X_i = 1 if person i gets their own hat. Each column of this table adds up to that order's count.
walk.look: Notice: the column for 123 is 1, 1, 1 (total 3), matching the count above.

walk.say: Look along one row. X_1 is 1 in 2 of the 6 orders, so Pr[X_1 = 1] = 1/3, and by the warm-up E[X_1] = 1/3. Person 1's hat is equally likely to be any of the 3 hats.
walk.look: Notice: two 1s in a row of six.

walk.say: Every row looks the same: E[X_1] = E[X_2] = E[X_3] = 1/3. Linearity: E[X] = 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1, matching the brute force.

visual.caption: adding rows = adding columns: both give 1

walk.look: Notice: the rows depend on each other (if two people match, so does the third), yet we just add.

walk.say: For any n: each person's hat is uniformly one of n hats, so E[X_i] = 1/n. There are n people, so E[X] = n × 1/n = 1.
walk.look: Notice: n cancels. The answer doesn't depend on n at all.

walk.say: Answer: the expected number of people who get their own hat is exactly 1, for every n. For n = 3 the six orders average (3+1+1+0+0+1)/6 = 1.

visual.caption: checked by listing every order

walk.look: Notice: 120 orders for n = 5, and the average is still 1.

problems.why: The X_i depend on each other, but linearity of expectation doesn't care: E[X_1 + ... + X_n] = E[X_1] + ... + E[X_n] always. Split the count into 0/1 indicators, find each one's probability, add.
problems.tip: If a question asks for the expected number of something, write it as a sum of indicator variables before doing anything else.

problems.title: Waiting for success and the coupon collector
problems.problem: (a) A trial succeeds with probability p, independently each time. Show the expected number of trials up to and including the first success is 1/p. (b) Rolling a fair die, what is the expected number of rolls until every face has appeared?

visual.caption: Keep rolling until you have seen all six faces.

warmup.question: Flip a fair coin until it lands heads. What is the chance it takes exactly 3 flips?
warmup.answer: You need tails, tails, heads: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

walk.say: (a) The first success is on trial j when the first j - 1 trials fail and trial j succeeds: (1 - p)^(j-1) p. With p = 1/2 that is 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ...
walk.look: Notice: each step multiplies by another failure, (1 - p).

walk.say: E[X] = sum over j of j × Pr[first success at j] = sum of j (1 - p)^(j-1) p = p × 1/p^2 = 1/p. With p = 1/2 the running total heads to 2.

visual.caption: 1/p = 2 tries on average

walk.look: Notice: the totals creep up to 2 = 1/p and never pass it.

walk.say: (b) Cut the rolls into phases. Phase j runs while exactly j different faces have been seen, j = 0, ..., 5. In phase j a roll is new with probability (6 - j)/6.
walk.look: Notice: the chance of something new keeps shrinking.

walk.say: Inside one phase the chance p is fixed, so by part (a) the phase lasts 1/p = 6/(6 - j) rolls on average.
walk.look: Notice: the last phase alone takes 6 rolls on average.
Notice: the last two phases take 9 of the 14.7 rolls.

walk.say: Answer: (a) 1/p trials. (b) 14.7 rolls on average. In general, collecting all n coupons takes n H_n, about n ln n, draws.

visual.caption: grows like n ln n

walk.look: Notice: 6 faces need 14.7 rolls, far more than 6.

problems.why: Waiting time is 1/p, so rare events take long to wait for. The coupon collector is mostly spent waiting for the last few coupons, when p is small. Splitting into phases where p is fixed, then adding with linearity, turns a messy process into a simple sum.
problems.tip: Whenever 'p' changes as you go, cut the process into phases where p is fixed and add up 1/p for each phase.

problems.title: Contention resolution
problems.problem: n processes share one resource. Each round, every process tries to use it with probability 1/n, and an attempt succeeds only if nobody else tries. How likely is a given process to succeed in one round? About how many rounds until it has succeeded with good probability?

visual.caption: What must happen for P_i to win this round?

warmup.question: Two independent events have chances 1/2 and 1/3. What is the chance that both happen?
warmup.answer: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. For independent events, 'all of them happen' means multiply.

walk.say: Process i wins a round when it tries (chance 1/n) and each of the other n - 1 processes waits (chance 1 - 1/n each).
walk.look: Notice: one 'tries' and n - 1 'waits', all needed at once.

walk.say: The processes choose independently, so multiply: Pr[win] = (1/n)(1 - 1/n)^(n-1). For n = 4: (1/4)(3/4)^3 = 27/256, about 0.105.
walk.look: Notice: the waiting part (3/4)^3 is about 0.42.

walk.say: How big is (1 - 1/n)^(n-1)? It starts at 1/2 for n = 2 and slides down toward 1/e, about 0.37, but never below it.
walk.look: Notice: the teal curve stays above the dashed 1/e line.

walk.say: So Pr[win in one round] >= 1/(en). For n = 4 the exact 0.105 beats the bound 0.092; for n = 100 it is 0.003697 vs 0.003679, almost equal.
walk.look: Notice: the bound gets tight as n grows.

walk.say: Failing t rounds in a row has chance at most (1 - 1/(en))^t <= e^(-t/(en)). After t = en rounds that is at most 1/e. For n = 4, en is about 10.9 rounds.
walk.look: Notice: the curve is at 1/e where the marker sits, and keeps dropping.

walk.say: Answer: one round succeeds with probability (1/n)(1 - 1/n)^(n-1) >= 1/(en). After en rounds failure is at most 1/e, and after en × c ln n rounds it is at most e^(-c ln n) = n^(-c).
walk.look: Notice: doubling the rounds squares the failure chance.

problems.why: Choosing p = 1/n balances 'try often enough' with 'don't collide'. Two facts do most of the work in this chapter: (1 - 1/n)^n heads to 1/e, and repeating a chance-p event about 1/p times makes it likely to have happened.
problems.tip: 'All of these independent things happen' means multiply their probabilities. Then reach for (1 - 1/n)^(n-1) >= 1/e.

problems.title: Amplifying a Monte Carlo algorithm
problems.problem: A randomized algorithm finds the right answer with probability at least p = 1/4, and you can always tell when it has (for example, it outputs a valid witness). How many independent runs make the failure chance at most 1/1000?

visual.caption: You only lose if every run fails.

warmup.question: One run fails with probability 1/2. Two independent runs: what is the chance both fail?
warmup.answer: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Independent failures multiply, so each extra run shrinks the failure chance.

walk.say: You lose only if all k runs fail. They are independent, so Pr[all fail] <= (3/4)^k. Watch how fast it shrinks.
walk.look: Notice: 16 runs already push it near 1%.

walk.say: Solving (3/4)^k <= 1/1000 needs logs of 3/4. Easier: use 1 - x <= e^(-x), true for every x. So (1 - p)^k <= e^(-pk).
walk.look: Notice: the straight line 1 - x never rises above the curve e^(-x).

walk.say: Now set e^(-k/4) <= 1/1000. Take ln: k/4 >= ln 1000, about 6.91, so k >= 27.6. Round up: 28 runs.
walk.look: Notice: the exact curve (pink) sits under the easy bound (dashed).

walk.say: Check exactly: (3/4)^24 is about 0.00100, just over 1/1000, while (3/4)^25 is about 0.00075. So 25 is the true minimum; the e-bound asks for 28, a bit cautious but easy.
walk.look: Notice: the bound is always the bigger number in each column.

walk.say: Answer: 28 runs (by the bound; 25 exactly) make failure at most 1/1000. In general k = (1/p) ln(1/δ) runs push it below δ.
walk.look: Notice: a thousand times safer costs only about 28 more runs.

problems.why: Repeating multiplies the failure chances, so they shrink exponentially in the number of runs. 1/p runs bring failure down to about 1/e, and every further 1/p runs buys another factor of e. This is how Karger's algorithm goes from 'rarely works' to 'almost always works'.
problems.tip: Memorize 1 - x <= e^(-x). It turns '(1 - p)^k is small' into 'k >= (1/p) ln(1/δ)' in one line.

problems.title: Karger's min cut success probability
problems.problem: Karger's algorithm repeatedly contracts a uniformly random edge until 2 nodes are left, and outputs the edges between them. Show it finds a given min cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)). Use two triangles joined by one edge (n = 6) as the example.

visual.caption: Two triangles joined by one edge: the min cut is c-d (k = 1).

warmup.question: This graph has 7 edges, and exactly 1 of them (c-d) is in the min cut. You pick one edge uniformly at random. What is the chance you pick c-d?
warmup.answer: 1/7. Each of the 7 edges is equally likely, and only one of them is the cut edge.

walk.say: One run, step by step. Contract a random edge, say a-b: merge the two ends into one node, keep any parallel edges, and throw away self-loops. ab now has two edges to c.
walk.look: Notice: the coral cut edge c-d is still there. That's all we need.

walk.say: Next random pick: e-f. They merge into ef, which now has two edges to d.
walk.look: Notice: 4 nodes and 5 edges left, and c-d is 1 of the 5.

walk.say: Next: one of the two ab-c edges. ab and c merge into abc; the other ab-c edge becomes a self-loop and is thrown away.
walk.look: Notice: now 1 of only 3 edges is the cut edge. The danger grows as the graph shrinks.

walk.say: Next: one of the two d-ef edges. Two nodes are left, abc and def, joined by 1 edge. This run found the min cut, because it never picked c-d.

visual.caption: output: 1 edge = the min cut

walk.look: Notice: the run succeeds exactly when no cut edge is ever contracted.

walk.say: Why the cut usually survives: if the min cut has k edges, every node has degree >= k (or that node alone would be a smaller cut), so m >= kn/2. So Pr[pick a cut edge] = k/m <= 2/n. Here: 1/7 <= 2/6.

visual.caption: k = 1, every degree >= 1, m = 7 >= 3

walk.look: Notice: lots of edges overall means a small chance of hitting the few cut edges.

walk.say: With j nodes left the same argument gives <= 2/j. So Pr[cut survives every step] >= (1 - 2/n)(1 - 2/(n-1)) ... (1 - 2/3). For n = 6: 4/6 × 3/5 × 2/4 × 1/3 = 1/15.
walk.look: Notice: the numerators 4, 3, 2, 1 and denominators 6, 5, 4, 3 mostly cancel.

walk.say: Answer: in general (n-2)/n × (n-3)/(n-1) × ... × 2/4 × 1/3 telescopes to 2/(n(n-1)). For n = 6 that is 2/30 = 1/15, so one run finds the min cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)).

visual.caption: everything faded cancels; left: (2 × 1) / (n(n-1))

walk.look: Notice: only 2 and 1 survive on top, n and n-1 on the bottom.

problems.why: One run rarely succeeds, but each step only risks a 2/j chance, and those risks multiply into a telescoping product. Running it about (n^2/2) ln n times and keeping the smallest cut found makes failure at most about 1/n. A side effect: a graph has at most n(n-1)/2 distinct min cuts.
problems.tip: When each step fails with a small chance, the chance of never failing is a product of (1 - small) terms; look for it to telescope.

problems.title: Randomized quicksort's expected comparisons
problems.problem: Quicksort picks each pivot uniformly at random. Let z_1 < z_2 < ... < z_n be the sorted values. Show Pr[z_i and z_j are ever compared] = 2/(j - i + 1), and use it to show the expected number of comparisons is O(n log n). Compute it exactly for n = 4.

visual.caption: the values in sorted order (quicksort sees them shuffled)

warmup.question: Four values z_2, z_3, z_4, z_5 sit together, and one of them is picked uniformly at random. What is the chance it is one of the two ends, z_2 or z_5?
warmup.answer: 2/4 = 1/2. Two of the four equally likely picks are ends.

walk.say: Quicksort compares the pivot with everything in its piece, then splits the piece. Say the first pivot is z_3: it is compared with all five others, and then z_1, z_2 and z_4, z_5, z_6 are in different pieces forever.
walk.look: Notice: z_2 and z_5 can never be compared now. They were split up.

walk.say: So two values are compared only if one of them is a pivot while both are still in the same piece. Focus on the block z_i, ..., z_j: it stays together until the first pivot from inside it is chosen.
walk.look: Notice: pivots outside the block (z_1, z_6) don't split it.

walk.say: Every value in the block is equally likely to be that first pivot. If it is z_i or z_j, they get compared. If it is anything in between, they are split. So Pr = 2/(j - i + 1). For z_2, z_5: 2/4.
walk.look: Notice: the warm-up was exactly this: 2 good picks out of 4.

walk.say: Each pair is compared at most once, so the total is a sum of 0/1 indicators, one per pair. By linearity, E[comparisons] = sum over pairs of 2/(j - i + 1). For n = 4, fill in a table.
walk.look: Notice: neighbors (gap 1) are always compared: probability 2/2 = 1.

walk.say: Group by gap j - i. Gap 1: 3 pairs × 1 = 3. Gap 2: 2 pairs × 2/3 = 4/3. Gap 3: 1 pair × 1/2. Total 3 + 4/3 + 1/2 = 29/6, about 4.83.

visual.caption: teal gap 1, yellow gap 2, pink gap 3: total 29/6

walk.look: Notice: the worst case for n = 4 is 6 comparisons; the average is under 5.

walk.say: Answer: Pr = 2/(j - i + 1), and for n = 4 the expectation is 29/6. In general each row i adds at most 2(1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n) <= 2H_n, so the total is at most 2n H_n = O(n log n).
walk.look: Notice: the expected cost grows far slower than the worst case.

problems.why: Counting comparisons directly is messy, but each pair is compared at most once, so the total is a sum of 0/1 indicators. The whole analysis is one probability per pair plus linearity, and the harmonic sum H_n, about ln n, gives the log.
problems.tip: For 'expected number of comparisons/collisions/inversions', sum over pairs: E = sum of Pr[this pair is counted].

problems.title: Randomized selection in expected O(n)
problems.problem: Select(S, k) picks a random splitter, splits S into smaller and larger, and recurses into the one side that holds the k-th smallest. Show its expected running time is O(n).

visual.caption: ranks of 8 elements; the splitter is one of them, chosen at random

warmup.question: 8 elements with ranks 1 to 8. The splitter has rank 3. How many elements are smaller, and how many are larger?
warmup.answer: 2 smaller (ranks 1, 2) and 5 larger (ranks 4 to 8). Even if we recurse into the bigger side, only 5 of 8 remain.

walk.say: Call a splitter central if at least n/4 elements are below it and at least n/4 above. For n = 8 that is ranks 3 to 6: half of all elements, so Pr[central] = 1/2.
walk.look: Notice: we don't need the median, just something in the middle half.

walk.say: After a central splitter, whichever side we recurse into has at most 3n/4 elements. Worst central case for n = 8, rank 3: the larger side has 5 <= 6.
walk.look: Notice: at least a quarter of the elements are thrown away.

walk.say: Split the run into phases by size: phase j lasts while the size is between n(3/4)^(j+1) and n(3/4)^j. With n = 100: phase 0 is 75 to 100, phase 1 is 56 to 75, and so on.

visual.caption: phase j: size between 100(3/4)^(j+1) and 100(3/4)^j

walk.look: Notice: each phase's range is 3/4 as wide as the one before.

walk.say: A central splitter always ends the current phase. Each splitter is central with chance 1/2, so a phase lasts 1/p = 2 iterations on average. Each iteration in phase j costs at most c n (3/4)^j to split.
walk.look: Notice: the tries stay at 2, but the work per try keeps shrinking.
Notice: a geometric series is a constant times its first term.

walk.say: Answer: the expected running time is at most 8cn = O(n). Quicksort is O(n log n) because it recurses into both sides; selection keeps only one, so the work shrinks geometrically.
walk.look: Notice: one branch per level, each level smaller by 3/4.

problems.why: We don't need a perfect median, just a splitter that is 'good enough' half the time. Then the sizes shrink geometrically, and a geometric series is a constant times its first term, so the total stays linear.
problems.tip: To analyze 'keep trying until a good event', split the run into phases by size and use 'expected tries = 1/p' inside each phase.

practice.problem: Every clause has exactly 2 different variables, for example (x_1 ∨ ¬x_2). What is the expected fraction of clauses a random assignment satisfies? With k = 20 clauses, how many can you always satisfy at once?

visual.caption: Settings of x_1 x_2. Shade the ones that make (x_1 ∨ ¬x_2) false.

practice.hint: An OR clause fails only when every literal is false. How many of the 4 settings do that?
practice.answer: A 2-literal clause fails only when both literals are false: 1 setting of 4 (for (x_1 ∨ ¬x_2) that is x_1 = F, x_2 = T). So each clause is satisfied with probability 3/4, and by linearity E[satisfied] = 3k/4. For k = 20 that is 15, so some assignment satisfies at least 15 clauses.

practice.problem: You guess the cards of a shuffled n-card deck one at a time, and after each guess the card is shown. You always guess uniformly at random among the cards not yet shown. What is the expected number of correct guesses? Give the exact value for n = 4.

visual.caption: n = 4: fill in, then add the bottom row

practice.hint: Let X_i = 1 if guess i is right. On guess i, how many cards are still unseen, and how many of them are correct?
practice.answer: On guess i there are n - i + 1 unseen cards and you pick one uniformly, so Pr[X_i = 1] = 1/(n - i + 1). By linearity E[X] = 1/n + 1/(n - 1) + ... + 1/1 = H_n, about ln n. For n = 4: cards left 4, 3, 2, 1, so 1/4 + 1/3 + 1/2 + 1 = 25/12, about 2.08. (Guessing without using what you've seen gives only 1.)

practice.problem: (a) How many rolls of a fair die do you expect until the first 6? (b) A cereal has 4 different toys, each equally likely in every box. What is the expected number of boxes until you own all 4? Give the exact value.
practice.hint: Split into phases by how many toys you own. In each phase the chance of a new toy is fixed, so that phase takes 1/p boxes.
practice.answer: (a) p = 1/6, so 6 rolls on average. (b) Pr new = 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 1/4, so the phases take 1, 4/3, 2 and 4 boxes on average. Total 1 + 4/3 + 2 + 4 = 25/3, about 8.33 boxes. (That is 4 × H_4 = 4 × 25/12.)

practice.problem: With n = 5 processes each trying with probability 1/5, what is the exact chance a given process succeeds in one round? Compare it with 1/(en). Using the bound, after how many rounds is the chance it has never succeeded at most 1/e?

visual.caption: Fill in each chance, then multiply.

practice.hint: Write 1/5 under the process that tries and 4/5 under each one that waits. For the rounds, use e^(-t/(en)).
practice.answer: (1/5)(4/5)^4 = 256/3125, about 0.0819. The bound 1/(5e) is about 0.0736, so the bound holds. Never succeeding in t rounds has chance at most e^(-t/(5e)), which is 1/e at t = 5e, about 13.6: so 14 rounds.

practice.problem: Karger's algorithm finds a given min cut of a 10-node graph with probability at least 2/(10 × 9) = 1/45 per run. Using (1 - p)^k <= e^(-pk), how many runs (keeping the smallest cut found) make the chance of missing it at most 1/100? How many runs does the recipe (n^2/2) ln n give, and what failure chance?
practice.hint: Set e^(-k/45) <= 1/100 and take ln of both sides. For the recipe, plug n = 10 into (n^2/2) ln n and then into e^(-pk).
practice.answer: Need k/45 >= ln 100, about 4.61, so k >= 207.2: 208 runs. (The exact (44/45)^k drops below 1/100 at k = 205.) The recipe (n^2/2) ln n = 50 × ln 10, about 115 runs. Since 2/(n(n - 1)) >= 2/n^2, the failure chance is at most e^(-(2/n^2)(n^2/2) ln n) = e^(-ln n) = 1/n = 1/10.

practice.problem: For n = 5, what is Karger's lower bound on finding a given min cut in one run? Write out the survival factors. Roughly how many runs push the failure chance below 1/e?

visual.caption: fill in 1 - 2/j, then multiply

practice.hint: Write the factors (1 - 2/j) for j = 5, 4, 3 and multiply. For the runs, recall 1/p runs bring failure to about 1/e.
practice.answer: Factors 3/5, 2/4, 1/3; product 6/60 = 1/10 = 2/(5 × 4). Ten independent runs fail with probability at most (1 - 1/10)^10, about 0.35, which is below 1/e (about 0.37). So about 1/p = 10 runs.

practice.problem: Selection on n = 100 elements. Which ranks count as central splitters, what is the chance a random splitter is central, and at most how many elements remain after a central one? Why is the expected total work O(n) and not O(n log n)?

visual.caption: ranks 1 to 100: shade the central ones

practice.hint: A central splitter needs at least 25 elements below it and at least 25 above. Which ranks does that allow?
practice.answer: Central needs at least 25 elements on each side: ranks 26 through 75, which is 50 of the 100, so probability 1/2. At most 75 = 3n/4 elements remain. The work per phase shrinks by a factor 3/4 each time (100, 75, about 56, ...), with 2 iterations per phase on average, so the total is about 2c(100 + 75 + 56 + ...) <= 2c × 4 × 100 = 800c: a geometric series, linear in n. Quicksort is O(n log n) because it recurses into both sides.
